title: Evaluating strategies to optimize breast MRI screening: a modeling study of abbreviated protocols, dockable tables, and staffing scenarios.
abstract: Objective MRI is increasingly recommended for breast cancer screening, particularly in women with dense breast tissue. However, widespread adoption is constrained by limited capacity and high costs. This study evaluated how optimized MRI screening workflows could address these barriers through three targeted interventions: an abbreviated scan protocol, dockable MRI tables, and expanded technician staffing. Materials and methods A calculation model was developed to compare seven workflow strategies against the current standard care. Strategies included reducing MRI acquisition time from 13 to 6 min, introducing dockable tables with breast coils, adding a third technician, and combinations thereof. Workflow durations and cost inputs were derived from published literature, hospital data, and expert opinion. Primary outcomes were daily screening capacity, cost per screening, annual screening costs, and staffing requirements for a screening volume of 5500 screening examinations per year. Results After evaluating several optimized workflow strategies, we found that reducing MRI acquisition time increased daily screening capacity from 30 to 47 scans, with associated annual savings of €147,505 (8.4%) and a reduction of 1320 technician hours. Combined strategies integrating reduced scan time, additional technicians, and dockable tables increased the daily capacity from 30 to 67 scans and reduced annual costs by up to €160,557 (9.2%) compared with the current workflow. Conclusions Optimizing MRI breast cancer screening workflows with abbreviated scan protocols and dockable tables can substantially increase screening capacity, reduce costs, and technician workload. This would expand access to MRI screening, without requiring additional scanners, potentially providing a solution for (future) capacity problems. Key points Question Which workflow optimization strategies, including abbreviated scan protocols, dockable tables, and additional technicians, offer the greatest capacity and cost benefits for MRI breast cancer screening? Findings Abbreviated scan protocols provide the largest cost savings, while combined workflow changes can substantially increase capacity and still reduce costs. Clinical relevance Optimizing MRI breast cancer screening workflows with abbreviated scans and dockable tables can increase screening capacity and reduce costs and technician workload. This expands access to MRI screening, without requiring additional scanners, potentially providing a solution for capacity problems.

title: Delayed hepatobiliary phase imaging improves bile leak detection on gadoxetate-enhanced MRI.
abstract: Objectives To compare conventional and delayed (≥ 30 min) hepatobiliary-phase (HBP) gadoxetate-enhanced MRI for the detection of bile leaks. Materials and methods This retrospective single-center study included all consecutive gadoxetate-enhanced MRI examinations comprising delayed HBP acquisitions performed for suspected biliary leak over 2 years at a tertiary hepatobiliary referral center. Two abdominal radiologists blinded to clinical records independently assessed leak presence at each timepoint. title: AI for reducing claims and compensation payments from missed fractures on radiographs.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the potential of BoneView, an artificial intelligence (AI) tool for fracture detection on radiographs in claims cases related to missed fractures that resulted in financial compensation. Materials and methods This retrospective, multicenter study included all patients who submitted a claim and received financial compensation for missed fractures on radiographs between January 2013 and December 2019 across the 38 university hospitals of the Greater Paris area (AP-HP-France). For each claimant, 5 control patients were selected from a contemporary single-center cohort of patients who underwent radiographs of the same anatomical regions (with or without fracture) performed in the emergency department of a university hospital, irrespective of fracture status. Three radiologists (musculoskeletal fellow, 5-year fellowship-trained radiologist, and > 20-year expert) independently performed blinded, unassisted, and AI-assisted interpretations following a 3-month washout. Sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were calculated with and without AI and for standalone AI. Compensation amounts were used to estimate potentially avoidable payouts. Results 156 patients (mean age, 42.2 years; 113 (72.4%) males), including 26 claimants with missed fractures on radiographs and 130 controls, were evaluated. 27/130 (20.8%) of the control cohort had fractures. Standalone AI sensitivity was 80.8% (21/26; 95% CI [60.7-93.5]) for claimants and 96.3% (26/27; 95% CI [81.0-99.9]) for the control cohort (p = 0.10). AI assistance did not significantly improve sensitivity, with expert reader sensitivity increasing from 81.1% to 92.5% (p = 0.10). Total compensation was €282,850 (€10,878 per case). AI-assisted detection could have potentially mitigated €265,314, representing a 93.8% theoretical reduction in institutional financial liability. Conclusion AI-assisted fracture detection identified most missed fractures on radiographs leading to compensation and may help reduce medicolegal risk and compensation-related financial burden. Key points Question Can AI-assisted fracture detection identify fractures missed by radiologists on radiographs that led to compensated medicolegal claims and institutional financial liability? Findings Standalone AI detected 21/26 (80.8%) of missed fractures in patients with compensated claims, corresponding to €265,314/€282,850 (93.8%) of total compensation in this cohort. Clinical relevance AI-assisted fracture detection can potentially increase radiologists' diagnostic accuracy and reduce medicolegal risk and compensation-related financial burden. Implementing AI tools in emergency settings may significantly mitigate patient harm and institutional costs associated with missed fractures.

title: Evolving role of cryoablation and cryoneurolysis for interventional pain management.
abstract: Despite advances in pain management, pain remains a major global health challenge in both oncological and non-oncological patients. Long-term pharmacological treatment is often restricted by insufficient therapeutic benefit and adverse events, highlighting the need for alternative approaches such as image-guided pain therapies. The idea of treating pain with cold has been recognized for centuries, and today cryotherapy has emerged as a valuable minimally invasive option for pain management. Cryoablation refers to the destruction of tissue with extreme cold and has an increasing role, especially in the treatment of benign (e.g., osteoid osteoma), malignant bone (i.e., metastases), and soft tissue tumors, either with a curative or palliative intent. Cryoneurolysis is a related but distinct application, focusing either on peripheral nerve modulation or nerve destruction. Cryoneurolysis may be highly effective for the treatment of acute or chronic pain, including sympathetic neurolysis in cancer and non-cancer-related pain syndromes. The general approach in patients with tumor-related pain depends on whether the lesion itself can be ablated or not. In non-oncologic patients, cryoneurolysis of the responsible nerve is typically performed following a positive response to a diagnostic nerve block. Potential indications for cryotherapy are constantly evolving; however, evidence, especially for cryoneurolysis, is still limited and based mostly on single-center case series and retrospective studies. Standardized ablation protocols are lacking, and for the duration of cycles, most experts rely on imaging visualization and validated protocols. Equally important, successful integration of cryoablation and cryoneurolysis into daily practice requires structured workflows across different patient pathways and interdisciplinary management. KEY POINTS: Question Pain management remains a major global health challenge and an unmet need in oncological and non-oncological patients. Findings Cryotherapy, in terms of cryoablation and cryoneurolysis, is increasingly incorporated in multimodal curative and palliative pain care concepts, for treatment of acute and chronic pain syndromes. Clinical relevance Advancement and validation of standardized treatment protocols are needed to strengthen evidence and further enhance clinical implementation in interventional radiology practice and interdisciplinary patient care.

title: Commercially available AI medical devices for prostate MRI: current evidence and opportunities for implementation.
abstract: Objective Artificial intelligence (AI) may improve prostate MRI interpretation and reduce radiologist workload, but evidence supporting clinical implementation remains limited. This scoping review summarises evidence on commercially available AI medical devices for prostate MRI. Materials and methods PubMed was searched for studies published through October 1, 2026. Eligible devices were cleared by the United States Food and Drug Administration and/or CE marked, with commercial availability corroborated through manufacturer websites. Data extraction addressed standalone AI performance, AI-assisted radiologist performance, workflow efficiency, and downstream clinical impact. Results Twenty-one studies evaluating 7 commercial AI systems were included; 17/21 (81%) were retrospective and 14/21 (67%) were single-centre. AI assistance suggested greater benefit for less-experienced readers, but improvements were inconsistent and increased specificity sometimes accompanied reduced sensitivity. Standalone evaluations, outside the devices' approved intended use, showed discrimination comparable to that of radiologists in selected cohorts. Inter-reader agreement and workflow benefits were mixed. We identify three key limitations of the current body of evidence that require thoughtful consideration before routine implementation: (1) incomplete verification strategies, (2) limited determination of workflow benefit, and (3) lack of analyses of cost-effectiveness and patient outcomes, e.g., time to treat or cancer-free survival. Conclusion Evidence supporting the use of commercial AI for prostate MRI remains limited and heterogeneous, with inconsistent diagnostic benefits. Prospective comparative studies in real clinical workflows are needed to determine its potential role within the prostate cancer diagnostic pathway. Key points Question Evidence for clinical implementation of prostate AI remains limited-most studies are retrospective and single-centre, with heterogeneous populations and reference standards. Findings AI may improve diagnostic performance for less-experienced readers, but gains for expert readers and assessment of workflow efficiency are limited. Clinical relevance Prospective multicentre studies embedded in real-world pathways are needed, together with analyses of cost-effectiveness and patient outcomes.

title: Systolic pressure gradient across myocardial bridge mediates the effect of bridge depth on clinical symptoms.
abstract: Objective The relationship between myocardial bridging (MB) morphology and function and the pathways to clinical symptoms remained unclear. This study investigated the association between delta coronary computed tomographic angiography-derived fractional flow reserve (ΔCT-FFR) and angina-equivalent symptoms in left anterior descending MB without coronary atherosclerosis using photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT). Materials and methods This retrospective cohort included 180 patients with deep MB (depth > 2 mm) and no plaques. All underwent PCD-CT angiography. CT-FFR was computed by machine learning; systolic (ΔCT-FFRsys) and diastolic (ΔCT-FFRdia) trans-bridge pressure gradients were derived. MB depth and length were measured. Associations with symptoms were assessed by logistic regression and mediation analysis. Results Symptomatic patients (n = 81) had greater depth (median 3.30 mm vs. 2.45 mm), longer length (mean 36.06 mm vs. 26.10 mm), higher ΔCT-FFRsys (3.81% vs. 1.62%) and ΔCT-FFRdia (3.45% vs. 2.15%) than asymptomatic patients (n = 99) (all p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis identified depth (OR = 1.77, 95% CI: 1.27-2.46, p = 0.001) and ΔCT-FFRsys (OR = 1.16, 95% CI: 1.05-1.27, p = 0.002) as independent predictors. Mediation analysis indicated that ΔCT-FFRsys significantly mediated the effect of depth on symptoms (indirect effect = 0.1881, 95% CI: 0.1023-0.2897). Conclusions MB depth and ΔCT-FFRsys were independent risk factors for symptoms, and ΔCT-FFRsys appeared to mediate the morphological-clinical symptoms link. These findings suggested that integrated assessment, particularly ΔCT-FFRsys, might be a new non-invasive imaging biomarker for clinically identify symptomatic MB and understand its potential pathogenic mechanisms. Key points Question The precise relationship between myocardial bridging morphological and functional features and clinical symptoms, and whether underlying key mediating factors exist, remains currently incompletely determined. Findings Depth, length, and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient of myocardial bridging independently predicted symptoms, with the gradient significantly mediating the relationship between morphology and clinical presentation. Clinical relevance Noninvasive assessment of depth and systolic trans-bridge pressure gradient can assist in identifying patients with symptomatic myocardial bridging, serving as potential imaging biomarkers and providing insights into the underlying pathophysiology of symptom presentation.

title: Ultrasound quantification of liver fat in MASLD.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is highly prevalent and frequently first recognized at ultrasound, but conventional B-mode assessment is limited by subjectivity and reduced sensitivity for mild steatosis. Quantitative ultrasound (QUS) techniques address these limitations by converting acoustic signal properties into numerical biomarkers of hepatic fat, including attenuation coefficient, backscatter coefficient, speed of sound, and composite measures. This review summarizes the technical principles, current evidence, clinical implementation, and limitations of ultrasound-based liver fat quantification techniques in MASLD. Their major advantages are accessibility, integration into routine ultrasound examinations, and potential use alongside elastography for multiparametric assessment. However, thresholds vary across vendors, software implementations, acquisition protocols, reference standards, and patient populations, limiting interchangeability and universal cutoffs. In clinical practice, ultrasound fat quantification should not be interpreted in isolation but integrated with fibrosis risk stratification and metabolic risk assessment. Further multicenter studies are needed to standardize acquisition and reporting, define clinically meaningful longitudinal changes, and link ultrasound-derived fat reduction with patient outcomes. QUS is therefore best regarded as an evolving, practical framework for objective steatosis assessment that complements, rather than replaces, comprehensive MASLD risk stratification. KEY POINTS: Question Conventional B-mode ultrasound is subjective and insensitive to mild hepatic steatosis, creating an unmet need for objective, reproducible liver fat quantification in MASLD. Findings Attenuation-based and composite quantitative ultrasound methods provide objective liver fat assessment, but vendor-dependent thresholds currently limit interchangeability and universal clinical application. Clinical relevance Quantitative ultrasound enables accessible, objective liver fat assessment during routine imaging, improving detection and grading of hepatic steatosis and supporting risk-based MASLD care; however, vendor-specific thresholds and acquisition variability require technique-specific interpretation.

title: Detection of recurrence after surgical treatment for urachal adenocarcinoma: diagnostic yield of cystoscopy, imaging and serum tumor markers.
abstract: Purpose Recurrence after surgical treatment of urachal adenocarcinoma (UrAC) occurs in up to 60% of patients, yet evidence-based surveillance strategies are lacking. We evaluated, which diagnostic modality first detected local and distant recurrence after surgery for UrAC and determined their yield to inform evidence-based follow-up. Methods We identified 65 consecutive patients from our prospectively maintained database (1994-2022) who were surgically treated with partial or total cystectomy. Routine follow-up up to 10 years consisted of cystoscopy, serum tumor-markers (STMs - CEA and/or CA19-9) and CT-scan according to our institutional protocol. Diagnostic yield was calculated as the number of recurrences detected until first recurrence divided by the number of examinations performed. Results Of the 65 patients, 33 (51%) developed a recurrence. Isolated local recurrence occurred in four patients (6%), while 29 patients (45%) developed distant recurrence. Recurrence was first detected by symptoms in 39% of patients and by routine follow-up in 61%. Routine cystoscopy detected local recurrence in 2 of 304 examinations; Both patients had simultaneous distant recurrence. For distant recurrence, CT and STMs detected recurrence first in 38%(11/29) and in 28%(8/29) patients, respectively. Conclusion Recurrence after surgery for UrAC is common and predominantly distant. Cross-sectional imaging and STMs contribute most to recurrence detection, whereas routine cystoscopic surveillance rarely detected isolated local recurrence.

title: Too good to be true? AI performance in CT-based urinary stone detection and classification: EAU endourology systematic review and diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate pooled performance of artificial intelligence (AI) in computed tomography (CT)-based urinary stone detection and classification and identify methodological factors influencing results. Methods This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261319940). A systematic search of PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar was conducted up to March 15, 2026. Studies evaluating AI-based detection or classification of urolithiasis on CT with available validation/test cohort data (sensitivity/specificity or 2 × 2 tables) were included. A bivariate random-effects model generated pooled sensitivity, specificity, and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) curves. Meta-regression explored moderators related to dataset composition and AI pipelines. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-AI. Results 14 studies (five detection-based, nine classification-based) were included. Overall pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.967 and 0.979 (AUC 0.987). Classification studies demonstrated higher pooled sensitivity (0.977) and specificity (0.990) compared with detection studies (0.935 and 0.919; AUC 0.945). Significant heterogeneity was observed and influenced by training sample size, class imbalance, presence of bladder stones or other pathologies, and architectural choices. Most studies had high risk of bias, lacked external validation, and frequently used slice-level or pre-selected datasets, potentially overestimating performance. Conclusion Substantial methodological heterogeneity and high risk of bias limit clinical generalizability. Detection studies better reflect real-world workflows and show lower performance. Current evidence does not support routine clinical implementation without standardized reporting and robust external validation.

Purpose

To evaluate pooled performance of artificial intelligence (AI) in computed tomography (CT)-based urinary stone detection and classification and identify methodological factors influencing results.

Methods

This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261319940). A systematic search of PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar was conducted up to March 15, 2026. Studies evaluating AI-based detection or classification of urolithiasis on CT with available validation/test cohort data (sensitivity/specificity or 2 × 2 tables) were included. A bivariate random-effects model generated pooled sensitivity, specificity, and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) curves. Meta-regression explored moderators related to dataset composition and AI pipelines. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-AI.

Results

14 studies (five detection-based, nine classification-based) were included. Overall pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.967 and 0.979 (AUC 0.987). Classification studies demonstrated higher pooled sensitivity (0.977) and specificity (0.990) compared with detection studies (0.935 and 0.919; AUC 0.945). Significant heterogeneity was observed and influenced by training sample size, class imbalance, presence of bladder stones or other pathologies, and architectural choices. Most studies had high risk of bias, lacked external validation, and frequently used slice-level or pre-selected datasets, potentially overestimating performance.

Conclusion

Substantial methodological heterogeneity and high risk of bias limit clinical generalizability. Detection studies better reflect real-world workflows and show lower performance. Current evidence does not support routine clinical implementation without standardized reporting and robust external validation.

title: Non-transecting posteriorly augmented anastomotic ureteroplasty with lingual mucosal onlay grafts: 5-year multi-institutional experience in 52 cases.
abstract: Purpose Complex proximal or mid-ureteral strictures remain a reconstructive challenge, especially in patients with complete obstruction. We aimed to evaluate the short- to mid-term feasibility, safety, and efficacy of non-transecting posteriorly augmented anastomotic ureteroplasty with lingual mucosal onlay grafts (ntPAA-LMGU). Methods In this retrospective, multicentre study, we reviewed adults who underwent robot-assisted ntPAA-LMGU at three centres and had at least 6 months of follow-up. Primary surgical success required the absence of symptoms, the absence of radiographic evidence of recurrent stricture, and freedom from secondary intervention. Renal functional outcomes were assessed by changes in overall estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and serial eGFR values were analysed using a linear mixed-effects model. Results The procedure was completed robotically in all 52 patients. Ten patients (19%) had previously undergone ureteral reconstruction. Median stricture length was 3.0 cm (IQR 2.9), median graft length was 3.0 cm (IQR 2.0), and median graft width was 1.5 cm (IQR 0.3). Median operative time was 167 min (IQR 75), median estimated blood loss was 50 mL (IQR 30), and median postoperative hospital stay was 6 days (IQR 2). No open conversion or intraoperative complications occurred. At a median follow-up of 17 months (IQR 13), the renal functional success rate was 94% (49/52), and the surgical success rate was 94% (49/52). Postoperative complications occurred in six (12%) patients, including two Clavien-Dindo grade IIIa events. Conclusions ntPAA-LMGU is a safe, feasible, and effective reconstructive option for complex proximal or mid-ureteral strictures.

title: Intraoperative non-contact three-dimensional measurement of the facial recess using a 4K3D exoscope during cochlear implantation.
abstract: To evaluate the technical feasibility of 4K3D exoscope-based non-contact three-dimensional measurement of the facial recess and explore agreement with scale-calibrated two-dimensional ImageJ measurements in cadaveric specimens and preoperative CT measurements in patients undergoing cochlear implantation. The system used in this study combined an AINNOVI-100 exoscope with SurgeReal 3D Studio. Cadaveric feasibility assessment and method comparison included 10 temporal bones from eight formalin-fixed cadaveric heads. Three-dimensional measurements were compared with scale-calibrated two-dimensional ImageJ measurements. The prospective single-center cohort included 23 patients undergoing cochlear implantation. Intraoperative measurements were compared with preoperative high-resolution computed tomography measurements for exploratory agreement using absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficients and Bland-Altman analysis. Cadaveric intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.878 to 0.934. Mean model-generation time was 1.97 s, and the recorded workflow from reconstruction initiation to result storage lasted 46.07 s. 31 of 35 cadaveric measurement attempts were successful (88.6%), including 29 initial successes (82.9%); 4 attempts failed (11.4%). In the 23 clinical cases, agreement was strongest for facial recess width (intraclass correlation coefficient, 0.962). Angular limits of agreement were wider but remained within the stated ± 10° comparison margin in both cohorts. This study supports the feasibility of obtaining non-contact quantitative measurements of the exposed facial recess using a 4K3D exoscope. The observed agreement, particularly for facial recess width, and the short reconstruction and measurement times support further evaluation of this workflow for intraoperative anatomical documentation. Future studies should establish three-dimensional measurement accuracy and reproducibility and examine how the resulting information contributes to surgical decision-making.

Mean model-generation time was 1.97 s, and the recorded workflow from reconstruction initiation to result storage lasted 46.07 s. 31 of 35 cadaveric measurement attempts were successful (88.6%), including 29 initial successes (82.9%); 4 attempts failed (11.4%). In the 23 clinical cases, agreement was strongest for facial recess width (intraclass correlation coefficient, 0.962). Angular limits of agreement were wider but remained within the stated ± 10° comparison margin in both cohorts. This study supports the feasibility of obtaining non-contact quantitative measurements of the exposed facial recess using a 4K3D exoscope. The observed agreement, particularly for facial recess width, and the short reconstruction and measurement times support further evaluation of this workflow for intraoperative anatomical documentation. Future studies should establish three-dimensional measurement accuracy and reproducibility and examine how the resulting information contributes to surgical decision-making.

title: Perilymphatic enhancement suggestive of blood-labyrinthine barrier dysfunction in tumor-negative unilateral asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss on 10-minute postcontrast 3D heavily T2-weighted FLAIR MRI.
abstract: Purpose We hypothesized that a subset of patients with tumor-negative, nonacute unilateral asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss (ASNHL) would show occult perilymphatic enhancement suggestive of blood-labyrinthine barrier (BLB) dysfunction on 10-min postcontrast three-dimensional (3D) heavily T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (hvT2-FLAIR) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This study aimed to determine its detection rate and regional distribution. Methods This retrospective study included 25 adults with nonacute unilateral ASNHL who underwent 3-T inner-ear MRI after post-imaging exclusion of three vestibular schwannomas from 28 clinically eligible patients. Precontrast 3D FLAIR, precontrast 3D hvT2-FLAIR, and 10-min postcontrast 3D hvT2-FLAIR images were visually scored. Expert-reviewed automated segmentation generated regional normalized signal intensity (NSI), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and contrast-enhancement percentage (CEP). Results Postcontrast 3D hvT2-FLAIR showed definite asymmetric perilymphatic enhancement in 15 of 25 patients (60%), significantly exceeding precontrast 3D FLAIR (8%; p < 0.001) and precontrast 3D hvT2-FLAIR (16%; p = 0.002). Inter-reader agreement was nearly perfect (κ = 0.915). The affected ear exhibited higher NSI and CNR in the basal turn and vestibular complex, and CEP was higher only in the basal turn; these findings remained significant after false discovery rate correction. Basal-turn enhancement did not correlate with high-frequency audiometric asymmetry. Conclusion Ten-minute postcontrast 3D hvT2-FLAIR MRI frequently revealed asymmetric perilymphatic enhancement suggestive of BLB dysfunction in tumor-negative, nonacute unilateral ASNHL, particularly within the cochlear basal turn and vestibular complex. This exploratory finding provides additional inner-ear information beyond routine tumor-exclusion MRI and is compatible with altered BLB permeability, although its longitudinal significance remains to be established.

title: The orbito-pterygo-sphenoidal ligament/posterior septal artery complex as a dual-function anatomical reference for transethmoidal sphenoidotomy.
abstract: Introduction The superior turbinate and sphenoid ostium are commonly used landmarks for sphenoidotomy; however, they may be obscured in severe inflammatory conditions such as eosinophilic chronic rhinosinusitis (ECRS) or affected by anatomical variations. This study evaluated the orbito-pterygo-sphenoidal ligament/posterior septal artery (OPSL/PSA) complex-guided transethmoidal sphenoidotomy (TES) as an anatomy-based approach for sphenoid sinus entry and controlled inferior extension of anterior sphenoid wall (ASW) removal. Methods This retrospective study included patients with ECRS who underwent sphenoidotomy. Outcomes were compared between the OPSL/PSA complex-guided TES group (24 patients, 48 sides) and a conventional group (25 patients, 50 sides). The primary endpoint was postoperative residual inferior ASW height measured using computed tomography. Secondary endpoints included ASW width, intraoperative events, operative time, and postoperative exploratory outcomes. Results Postoperative residual inferior ASW height was significantly smaller in the OPSL/PSA complex-guided TES group than in the conventional group (-0.8 ± 1.8 vs. 1.5 ± 2.5 mm; p < 0.001). The difference remained significant after adjustment for potential confounders. Superior turbinate resection was not performed in the OPSL/PSA complex-guided TES group, whereas it was performed in 28.0% of sides in the conventional group. No statistically significant differences in operative time or PSA-related hemorrhage were observed between groups. Conclusions The OPSL/PSA complex-guided TES was associated with a greater extent of inferior ASW removal and less frequent superior turbinate resection, with no statistically significant differences in operative time or ​PSA-related hemorrhage between groups. The OPSL/PSA complex may serve as a complementary anatomical reference with a dual function: assisting sphenoid sinus entry and guiding controlled inferior ASW removal in patients with ECRS.

title: Predictive modeling of sex from proximal femoral morphometry using machine learning algorithms: a radiological study in Egyptian adults.
abstract: Sex estimation is a foundational step in forensic identification, and the proximal femur, whether assessed through direct skeletal measurement or radiographic imaging, has shown considerable promise as a durable, sexually dimorphic anatomical region for this purpose. Machine learning (ML) classifiers offer a flexible alternative to traditional discriminant function analysis, yet Egyptian data combining radiographic proximal femoral morphometry with supervised ML remain limited. Hence, this study aimed to develop and compare ML models for sex estimation from proximal femoral radiographic measurements in an adult Egyptian population. Digital pelvic radiographs of 306 Egyptian adults, 135 males and 171 females, aged ≥ 30 years, were retrospectively analyzed. Four proximal femoral measurements, femoral head diameter, femoral neck axis length, femoral neck width, and intertrochanteric distance, were obtained after confirming bilateral symmetry. Nine supervised algorithms were trained and evaluated using cross-validation together with an independent hold-out test set, with performance assessed through accuracy, F1-score, and receiver operating characteristic analysis. All four measurements differed significantly between sexes, with femoral head diameter showing the largest effect size and emerging as the dominant predictor across most models. The decision tree classifier achieved the highest test-set accuracy at 86% (F1-score = 0.83), followed by the multilayer perceptron at 83% (F1-score = 0.82), although sex-specific accuracy revealed nontrivial classification bias for most models, with only gradient boosting and AdaBoost remaining within the 5% bias threshold generally considered acceptable in forensic practice. Area under the curve values ranged between approximately 0.85 and 0.91 on the test set. These findings suggest that proximal femoral radiographic measurements, and femoral head diameter in particular, may offer a reliable and population-specific basis for ML-assisted sex estimation in Egyptian adults. However, sex-specific performance, not accuracy alone, should guide the choice of any model intended for forensic application.

title: Feasibility of reducing Angiofil<sup>®</sup> concentration in multiphase postmortem CT angiography and implications for iodine consumption and environmental sustainability : an observational study.
abstract: Background Postmortem CT angiography (PMCTA) is widely used in forensic medicine to evaluate the vascular system before autopsy. The contrast mixture of 3,500 ml paraffin and 210 ml Angiofil ® , originally proposed by Grabherr et al. for multiphase postmortem CT angiography (MPMCTA) approach, provides reliable global vascular opacification. Recent advances in CT detector technology, image reconstruction techniques, and growing environmental concerns have encouraged the investigation of alternative contrast-agent dilutions aimed to reduce iodine consumption. The aim of this observational study was to explore whether lower Angiofil ® concentrations could be used while preserving adequate vascular visualization and diagnostic image quality. Methods Thirty cases were evaluated using four progressively diluted Angiofil ® -paraffin mixtures containing 200 ml, 180 ml, 150 ml, and 120 ml of Angiofil ® in 3,500 ml of paraffin. Contrast enhancement was quantified by measuring Hounsfield units (HU) within regions of interest (ROIs) placed in the ascending thoracic aorta and compared with a clinical case. Image quality was independently assessed by an experienced forensic radiologist based on opacification of the ascending thoracic aorta. In addition, a dedicated evaluation of coronary artery lumen and wall visualization was performed. Results The mixture containing 200 ml of Angiofil ® showed no relevant improvement in image quality compared with the original dilution. A mixture containing 180 ml of Angiofil ® allowed excellent vascular assessment in individuals with a BMI > 35 kg/m², whereas 150 ml of Angiofil ® provided optimal image quality in individuals with a BMI ≤ 35 kg/m². The 120 ml mixture remained diagnostically acceptable in most cases but produced photon-starvation artifacts in individuals with high muscle mass or a BMI > 33 kg/m², limiting vascular assessment. Conclusion Adjusting the Angiofil ® -paraffin mixture according to body morphology using 180 ml of Angiofil ® for individuals with a BMI > 35 kg/m² and 150 ml for those with a BMI ≤ 35 kg/m² maintains excellent vascular visualization while substantially reducing iodine consumption. This optimization supports more environmentally sustainable PMCTA practice without compromising diagnostic image quality.

title: Semi-automated sex estimation from the cochlea on routine clinical CT: limited incremental value of curvature-based shape descriptors.
abstract: Background Sex estimation is fundamental in forensic anthropology and bioarchaeology, yet classical methods rely on skeletal elements that are often absent or poorly preserved. The bony labyrinth, enclosed within the petrous bone, is a promising alternative owing to its early maturation and taphonomic resistance, and cochlear shape has been reported to carry a sex-specific signal. However, most approaches depend on manual segmentation, micro-CT, or complex shape-analysis frameworks that limit routine applicability. Objective To evaluate the feasibility of a semi-automated method for sex estimation from the cochlea using standard clinical CT and automated OTOPLAN segmentation, and to quantify the contribution of shape descriptors beyond cochlear size alone. Materials and methods We analyzed 139 cochleae from 87 adults using clinical CT scans (slice thickness ≤ 0.6 mm). The three-dimensional lateral wall path was extracted with OTOPLAN; after normalization and resampling, curvature- and torsion-based descriptors and scalar cochlear metrics were computed to train a supervised classifier. Preprocessing, feature, and hyperparameter choices were optimized by Bayesian optimization within a nested cross-validation, so that model selection and performance estimation used separate data. Six feature configurations were compared, with all partitions made at the patient level and the whole procedure repeated over five random partitions. Results In nested cross-validation, the best configurations reached an area under the ROC curve (AUC-ROC) of approximately 0.71. A model using cochlear diameter as its sole predictor did not differ detectably from those combining size and shape descriptors (AUC-ROC 0.71, 95% CI 0.62-0.80) and gave the highest balanced accuracy (0.70), with a sensitivity of 0.71 and a specificity of 0.70. Configurations restricted to shape descriptors reached a median AUC-ROC of 0.59, with lower confidence limits at or just above chance level (0.50-0.51). Adding curvature to diameter changed the median AUC by + 0.011 (95% CI - 0.064 to + 0.107). Conclusion Sex-related information is recoverable from cochlear geometry on routine clinical CT using a semi-automated pipeline, but no incremental value of shape descriptors beyond cochlear size was detected. Although accuracy remains moderate, the approach is non-destructive, scalable, and clinically compatible, offering a potential adjunct for forensic anthropology and bioarchaeology when conventional methods are unavailable. This is not an identification method and is not validated as a stand-alone forensic tool: it was evaluated by internal validation only, on in vivo clinical CT.

Materials and methods

We analyzed 139 cochleae from 87 adults using clinical CT scans (slice thickness ≤ 0.6 mm). The three-dimensional lateral wall path was extracted with OTOPLAN; after normalization and resampling, curvature- and torsion-based descriptors and scalar cochlear metrics were computed to train a supervised classifier. Preprocessing, feature, and hyperparameter choices were optimized by Bayesian optimization within a nested cross-validation, so that model selection and performance estimation used separate data. Six feature configurations were compared, with all partitions made at the patient level and the whole procedure repeated over five random partitions.

Results

In nested cross-validation, the best configurations reached an area under the ROC curve (AUC-ROC) of approximately 0.71. A model using cochlear diameter as its sole predictor did not differ detectably from those combining size and shape descriptors (AUC-ROC 0.71, 95% CI 0.62-0.80) and gave the highest balanced accuracy (0.70), with a sensitivity of 0.71 and a specificity of 0.70. Configurations restricted to shape descriptors reached a median AUC-ROC of 0.59, with lower confidence limits at or just above chance level (0.50-0.51). Adding curvature to diameter changed the median AUC by + 0.011 (95% CI - 0.064 to + 0.107).

Conclusion

Sex-related information is recoverable from cochlear geometry on routine clinical CT using a semi-automated pipeline, but no incremental value of shape descriptors beyond cochlear size was detected. Although accuracy remains moderate, the approach is non-destructive, scalable, and clinically compatible, offering a potential adjunct for forensic anthropology and bioarchaeology when conventional methods are unavailable. This is not an identification method and is not validated as a stand-alone forensic tool: it was evaluated by internal validation only, on in vivo clinical CT.

title: Development and technical validation of a standardised CT image preprocessing workflow for reproducible AI for forensic anthropological applications.
abstract: The use of computed tomography (CT scans) images is increasing in forensic anthropology to address ethical, logistical, and preservation challenges related to physical cadaveric collections. However, preparing large volumes of medical images for artificial intelligence (AI) applications remains challenging, particularly in terms of standardisation and data privacy. The aim of this study is to develop an automated preprocessing workflow for CT images to support machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) applications in forensic anthropology research and education. A Python-based pipeline was designed in three stages: data de-identification and sorting, patient table removal, and bone windowing. A script was developed for de-identification, and a custom U-Net architecture was developed for both patient table removal and bone windowing. The workflow was developed and applied to CT thorax. Model performance was evaluated using standard metrics and compared with ground-truth models. DICOM metadata de-identification was performed as part of preprocessing; all predefined identifying attributes were successfully processed in the 200 DICOM files examined. The patient table removal model removed the table successfully in 96% of datasets (192/200) and achieved 99.94% accuracy on the original, non-augmented test images. The bone segmentation model achieved a Dice score of 93.12% and a precision of approximately 90%. The segmented 3D models showed high agreement with the ground-truth model, with minimal geometric deviation. We have proposed an integrated workflow that provides an ethical, efficient and standardised solution for de-identifying and preprocessing CT imaging data. It also enables the preprocessing of a scalable dataset for AI applications, thereby supporting the development of methodologies for the modern population, with future expansion to full-body scans and other imaging modalities.

title: Post-mortem CT angiography for fatal vascular lesions in forensic death investigation: a systematic review of diagnostic performance, added value, and pitfalls.
abstract: Purpose Post-mortem CT angiography (PMCTA) is increasingly used in forensic death investigation to assess vascular disease, haemorrhage, and traumatic or natural vascular causes of death. However, its practical value depends on the lesion being investigated, the angiographic protocol, and the way imaging findings are integrated with autopsy and pathology. This systematic review evaluated the diagnostic performance, added value, and main pitfalls of PMCTA for fatal vascular lesions. Methods PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane/CENTRAL were searched for human post-mortem studies evaluating PMCTA in forensic, medico-legal, coronial, or post-mortem settings. Eligible studies compared PMCTA with autopsy, histopathology, targeted vascular dissection, or autopsy-based consensus. Evidence was grouped according to practical forensic use, including coronary stenosis assessment, autopsy triage, global vascular lesion detection, haemorrhage-source localization, aortic or traumatic vascular injury assessment, coronary plaque characterization, and artifact-related pitfalls. Risk of bias was assessed using a QUADAS-2-based approach adapted to forensic PMCTA studies. Results The available evidence did not support unrestricted pooling of all fatal vascular lesions. PMCTA was used for different forensic questions, and only coronary stenosis provided data close to conventional diagnostic accuracy assessment. In this domain, available studies showed high specificity but only moderate sensitivity for critical stenosis. Autopsy-triage studies suggested that PMCTA may reduce or guide invasive autopsy in selected adult coronial workflows. Global comparison studies showed added value for vascular lesion detection, and haemorrhage-source studies suggested that PMCTA may help localize bleeding vessels. Evidence on fatal coronary plaque characterization is emerging. Pitfall studies showed that post-mortem clots, incomplete vascular filling, contrast leakage, and extravasation artifacts may mimic or obscure vascular pathology. Conclusion PMCTA is best interpreted as a complementary tool in forensic vascular death investigation rather than as a general substitute for autopsy. Its contribution is strongest when it answers a specific vascular question, such as documenting coronary stenosis, guiding autopsy, mapping vascular lesions, localizing haemorrhage, or supporting targeted histopathology. Careful correlation with autopsy, pathology, case circumstances, and protocol-related artifacts remains essential.

title: In vivo assessment of brain microstructure in patients with Huntington's disease using quantitative MRI.
abstract: Objectives Using multiparametric mapping (MPM), we assessed the integrity of cortical and subcortical regions across different stages of Huntington's disease (HD), relating the derived findings to genetic modifiers and clinical measures. Methods Sixteen premanifest patients with HD (PwHD pre ), ten manifesting PwHD (PwHD man ), and forty-two healthy controls (HC) underwent clinical examinations and a 3 T imaging. We derived quantitative MPM maps to perform voxel-based quantification (VBQ) and voxel-based morphometry (VBM). We assessed group differences by combining PwHD pre and PwHD man (PwHD total ) and by comparing PwHD pre and PwHD man with age- and sex-matched HC. Using correlation analysis, we investigated the link between MPM-derived findings, CAG repeat length, and clinical scores. Results PwHD man presented with reductions in all four quantitative MPM maps across the bilateral caudate nucleus and the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital gyri. We observed spatial overlap between VBQ- and VBM-derived findings, demonstrating widespread volume loss in PwHD man . PwHD pre showed reductions in certain quantitative maps within the frontal and temporal regions. Reduced MPM values correlated with clinical scores of HD severity. Interpretation The observed reductions across four MPM modalities in PwHD man are consistent with demyelination and neuronal loss, as supported by widespread volume loss. The reductions observed in PwHD pre indicate early demyelination and inflammation. In this study, we demonstrated the utility and clinical relevance of MPM for detecting microstructural alterations across different stages of HD. MPM can serve as a non-invasive biomarker of neurodegeneration in HD, providing insight into the pathological events underlying the observed neuronal loss.

title: Comparative evaluation of GPT 5.2 Pro and Gemini 3 Pro large multimodal models for retinal optical coherence tomography interpretation.
abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) capable of interpreting medical images are increasingly accessible to patients, yet their reliability for retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT) interpretation remains uncertain. This study evaluated the performance of two state-of-the-art LMMs in detecting OCT features and generating diagnostic interpretations. In this cross-sectional study, 330 publicly available retinal OCT B-scans spanning 12 diagnostic categories, including normal scans and common retinal diseases, were analyzed. Two commercially available LMMs (GPT 5.2 Pro and Gemini 3 Pro) were evaluated using zero-shot inference. Models were assessed separately for detection of nine predefined OCT features and for free-text diagnostic interpretation. Feature detection performance was measured using per-feature metrics and macro-averaged F1 scores, while diagnostic accuracy was assessed against expert-adjudicated reference standards. Gemini 3 Pro demonstrated higher feature detection performance than GPT 5.2 Pro (macro-averaged F1 score 0.558 vs. 0.472) and higher diagnostic accuracy (58.8% vs. 32.1%). Both models performed better for visually salient abnormalities but showed limited sensitivity for subtle structural features. Normal OCT scans were frequently misclassified as pathological, particularly by GPT 5.2 Pro, which failed to correctly identify any normal images. Recurrent, model-specific diagnostic biases and hallucinated diagnoses were observed. Although LMMs can extract clinically relevant information from OCT scans, their diagnostic reliability remains limited, with frequent overcalling of pathology and systematic biases. Given their increasing availability to patients, these limitations raise concerns about potential misinterpretation outside supervised clinical settings. Careful validation and clear usage boundaries are needed before such tools can be safely integrated into patient-facing workflows.

title: The integral role of artificial intelligence models in retinal detachment diagnostics: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Purpose Retinal detachment (RD) is a vision-threatening condition requiring prompt diagnosis and management to optimize visual outcomes. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models have demonstrated promising results in RD detection across multiple imaging modalities; however, concerns regarding heterogeneity, external validation, and real-world implementation remain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance and clinical applicability of AI models for RD diagnostics. Methods A comprehensive electronic search of PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and Google Scholar was conducted in April 2026. Studies evaluating ML or DL models for RD detection, classification, segmentation, screening, or prognostic assessment using any imaging modality were included. Two independent reviewers performed study screening, data extraction, and quality assessment using the QUADAS-2 and CLAIM tools. Quantitative syntheses were performed using a bivariate random-effects model to pool sensitivity and specificity, while a random-effects inverse-variance model was applied for diagnostic odds ratio (DOR). Subgroup analyses were conducted according to imaging modality and use of external validation status. Publication bias and small-study effects were assessed using Deeks' funnel plot asymmetry test. Results Sixty-six studies were included in the systematic review, of which 31 studies comprising 118,432 images were eligible for meta-analysis. Fundus photography was the most commonly used imaging modality, and DL approaches predominated. The pooled sensitivity was 0.93 (95% CI: 0.89-0.95) and specificity was 0.98 (95% CI: 0.96-0.99), with moderate between-study heterogeneity. The model-based positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) were 0.86 (95% CI: 0.71-0.94) and 0.99 (95% CI: 0.97-1.00), respectively. The SROC curve yielded an AUC of 0.982 and a normalized pAUC of 0.964, while the pooled DOR was 642.3 (95% CI: 264.5-1559.7). No significant publication bias or small-study effects were detected (P = 0.544). Conclusions This study provides the most up-to-date comprehensive quantitative synthesis of AI applications for RD diagnostics, demonstrating excellent overall diagnostic performance across multiple imaging modalities. Despite these promising results, limited external and real-world clinical validation, together with methodological heterogeneity, continue to restrict clinical translation. Future multicenter prospective studies with standardized validation and reporting frameworks are essential for safe and generalizable implementation of AI-assisted RD diagnostics.

title: Neuroendocrine neoplasms of the digestive system: challenges of biopsy diagnosis.
abstract: The diagnosis of digestive neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) is increasingly being made on endoscopic biopsies and endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration/biopsy (EUS-FNA/FNB) or ultrasound biopsies taken from metastases. Although current classification systems provide a robust and elaborate framework for categorizing NENs, their application to limited tissue biopsy samples often remains challenging. A major challenge is the accurate distinction between well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) and poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas (NECs), which is essential because of their markedly different prognostic and therapeutic implications. Additional challenges include reliable Ki-67 assessment, recognition of intratumoral heterogeneity, and identification of mixed neoplasms, including mixed neuroendocrine-non-neuroendocrine neoplasms (MiNENs) and amphicrine-like carcinoma (ALC)-a recently introduced and still poorly characterized category-and assignment of the primary site in metastatic disease using organ-associated immunohistochemical markers. Site-specific differences in morphology and immunophenotype further complicate biopsy interpretation and require integration of histological, immunohistochemical, clinical, and radiological findings. Although morphology remains the cornerstone of diagnosis, molecular testing is increasingly used in difficult cases to identify predictive biomarkers and potentially actionable genomic alterations. This review focuses on a practical biopsy-oriented diagnostic approach, discusses major diagnostic pitfalls, controversial and emerging concepts, and highlights the clinicopathological features of NENs across the digestive tract.

title: Microstructural alterations of human medial temporal lobe in dementia: volumetric and DTI findings correlate with cell number and neuropathology.
abstract: Volumetric and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) alterations in medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions are consistently reported in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, their biological basis remains poorly understood. We combined Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) metrics with cellular quantification and neuropathological burden assessment to investigate microstructural substrates underlying MTL imaging alterations in human donors with known cognitive and neuropathological status. Absolute cell numbers were quantified in a cohort of 54 brain donors using the isotropic fractionator, and postmortem MRI was performed on a subset of 18 fixed brain hemispheres. To assess microstructural brain alterations associated with disease progression, in vivo volumetric and DTI metrics were analyzed in 39 cognitively unimpaired controls (CU), 31 individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 14 patients with clinical AD dementia. In the postmortem cohort, MTL diffusivity metrics showed moderate negative correlations with total cell numbers. Mean, axial, and radial diffusivity positively correlated with Braak stage, whereas fractional anisotropy (FA) correlated negatively with CERAD score, linking diffusion alterations to AD-related pathology. In vivo MTL analyses revealed increased mean, axial, and radial diffusivity, and reduced FA in AD patients compared with both CU and MCI individuals. The MCI group exhibited intermediate alterations in diffusivity. Differences between in vivo and postmortem diffusion values were consistent with tissue fixation, temperature, and variations in acquisition protocols. Our findings suggest that diffusion MRI alterations in the MTL are associated with reduced cellularity and neuropathological burden, supporting the biological relevance of DTI metrics as markers of microstructural degeneration in AD.

title: The unfolding symphony: unraveling brain dynamics via data-driven multi-scale functional connectivity in task-state fMRI.
abstract: Task-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) can characterize both regional responses and changes in statistical dependence among distributed brain systems. This narrative review examines dynamic and multiscale connectivity within a broader framework that distinguishes task-modulated functional connectivity, trial-wise covariation, effective connectivity, and data-driven state analysis. Sliding-window correlation, hidden Markov models, and co-activation patterns are compared by their data representations, temporal assumptions, and computational procedures; graph representations can be combined with each of these strategies. We discuss supervised recurrent, transformer, and graph models alongside unsupervised state discovery, self-supervised representation learning, and emerging brain foundation models. Explainability requires evaluation of model attributions, including graph masks and perturbation-based analyses, rather than anatomical plausibility alone. The spatial framework includes whole-brain networks, subnetworks, atlas-defined regions of interest, and voxel- or layer-level measurements. Proposed links across these levels remain hypotheses: faster sampling of the blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signal does not directly resolve millisecond neural interactions, and resting-state or animal findings do not establish the corresponding mechanism during human tasks. Shared task-evoked responses, hemodynamic variability, motion, and analytical choices can all alter apparent connectivity. Progress therefore depends on matching the estimator to the scientific question, comparing against activation and static-connectivity baselines, and validating results across participants, sessions, and acquisition settings.

title: Associations between peripheral immune markers and brain morphometry in normal individuals.
abstract: Peripheral immune signaling may be associated with brain structure, but evidence in healthy adults remains limited. We conducted a cross-sectional exploratory study to examine associations between circulating immune-marker concentrations and regional cortical morphometry. Structural T1-weighted MRI and peripheral blood samples were obtained from 62 healthcare workers. Cortical volume, surface area, thickness, and mean curvature were extracted for 68 Desikan-Killiany regions using FreeSurfer. Nine peripheral immune markers were measured. Associations were assessed using Spearman rank correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction across 34 regions within each immune-marker, hemisphere, and morphometric-measure family. Associations surviving false discovery rate (FDR) correction in the analyses were further examined using exploratory sensitivity general linear model adjusted for age, sex, and the corresponding global morphometric measure (estimated total intracranial volume for volume and total cortical surface area for surface area). TGF-β1 was the only immune marker with regional associations surviving FDR correction. Higher TGF-β1 concentrations were positively associated with right frontal cortical surface area (Spearman's ρ = 0.367-0.443) and volume (ρ = 0.345-0.502), involving caudal middle frontal, rostral middle frontal, superior frontal, lateral orbitofrontal, and pars orbitalis regions. Exploratory covariate-adjusted sensitivity analyses yielded nominal p-values below 0.05 for right caudal middle frontal surface area (β = 1.609) and volume (β = 4.914), and right superior frontal surface area (β = 2.740) and volume (β = 10.939). No associations involving cortical thickness, mean curvature, or other immune markers survived FDR correction. In this pilot exploratory study of apparently healthy adults, peripheral TGF-β1 concentrations were associated with regional variation in right frontal cortical surface area and volume. These cross-sectional findings do not establish causality, underlying mechanisms, functional relevance, or clinical significance, but provide preliminary hypotheses for larger longitudinal studies of peripheral immune-brain associations.

title: Monitoring of pulmonary outcomes in paediatric cystic fibrosis patients treated with modulator therapy-a narrative review.
abstract: Recently introduced CFTR modulator drugs have transformed the disease trajectories in people with cystic fibrosis. Children with cystic fibrosis, who would once have experienced progressive lung damage and pulmonary function decline from early life onwards, now, when treated with effective modulators, appear to have preserved lung structure and pulmonary function using conventional monitoring tools. However, since cystic fibrosis lung disease may still progress despite effective therapy, early detection of disease manifestation, disease progression, and the tracking of treatment responses remain crucial. Monitoring of lung disease in the current era of CFTR modulators, therefore, poses a fundamental challenge for cystic fibrosis clinicians and researchers. This narrative review summarises currently available monitoring tools for paediatric cystic fibrosis patients. In children with cystic fibrosis receiving effective CFTR modulator therapy, spirometry remains an important component of pulmonary monitoring but may be insufficient to detect early or residual lung disease. Complementary approaches, including multiple-breath washout, oscillometry, and structural and functional lung imaging, can provide more sensitive assessment of pulmonary abnormalities and treatment responses. Further development of sensitive, non-invasive biomarkers of airway infection and inflammation, alongside evidence to guide the integration of these tools into routine clinical care, remains an important priority. • CFTR modulator therapy has transformed clinical outcomes in cystic fibrosis, and children initiating effective modulators early in life frequently maintain normal or near-normal pulmonary function. • Conventional monitoring with spirometry, particularly FEV₁, has limited sensitivity for detecting early or residual cystic fibrosis lung disease. • Clinical monitoring of cystic fibrosis lung disease in children has shifted towards the use of technologies allowing for detection of subtle, potentially reversible, structural, functional, and inflammatory abnormalities that may persist despite modulator therapy. • Multiple-breath washout, quantitative computed tomography (CT), functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the chest, as well as emerging biomarkers provide complementary information beyond spirometry and are reshaping contemporary monitoring of CF lung disease.

title: Coronary artery calcification is not associated with survival in advanced gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancer: a secondary analysis of the EXPAND trial.
abstract: Purpose Computed tomography (CT) is the clinical standard for staging of gastrointestinal cancer. Previous studies have highlighted the prognostic significance of coronary artery calcification (CAC) detected by CT in various types of cancer. However, the prognostic role of CAC scoring in gastrointestinal cancers is still unclear. The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of CT-defined CAC on overall survival (OS) in patients with advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer. Methods CAC was semiquantitatively measured using the visual Weston method on baseline CT scans in 785 patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer from the phase III EXPAND trial. This present study is a secondary analysis of the base line CT images. In the original analysis patients were randomly assigned to first-line treatment with cisplatin/capecitabin ± cetuximab. The primary endpoint of the current subanalysis is the OS. For statistical analysis group differences were calculated using the Mann-Whitney-U test and ANOVA test. Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox regression analysis were used to test the effect of CAC on mortality. Results The median CAC score was 1 (IQR 0; 3). A total of 337 patients (42.9%) had no visible CAC (CAC score 0). Male patients had statistically significant higher CAC score compared to female patients (median 1 versus 0, p < 0.0001). In univariable Cox regression CAC showed no significant association with survival when analysed as a continuous value (HR: 0.99, 95% CI: 0.96-1.02, p = 0.74), and when dichotomized for absence and presence of calcification (HR:1.08, 95% CI: 0.92-1.26, p = 0.34). Similar results were identified in further subgroup analyses. Conclusion CT-defined CAC scoring has no relevant prognostic impact in advanced gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancer undergoing first-line chemotherapy. The present study cannot confirm the promising results for CAC scoring in lung cancer patients.

Purpose

Computed tomography (CT) is the clinical standard for staging of gastrointestinal cancer. Previous studies have highlighted the prognostic significance of coronary artery calcification (CAC) detected by CT in various types of cancer. However, the prognostic role of CAC scoring in gastrointestinal cancers is still unclear. The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of CT-defined CAC on overall survival (OS) in patients with advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer.

Methods

CAC was semiquantitatively measured using the visual Weston method on baseline CT scans in 785 patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer from the phase III EXPAND trial. This present study is a secondary analysis of the base line CT images. In the original analysis patients were randomly assigned to first-line treatment with cisplatin/capecitabin ± cetuximab. The primary endpoint of the current subanalysis is the OS. For statistical analysis group differences were calculated using the Mann-Whitney-U test and ANOVA test. Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox regression analysis were used to test the effect of CAC on mortality.

Results

The median CAC score was 1 (IQR 0; 3). A total of 337 patients (42.9%) had no visible CAC (CAC score 0). Male patients had statistically significant higher CAC score compared to female patients (median 1 versus 0, p < 0.0001). Conclusion

title: Multifocal intradural extramedullary myxopapillary ependymoma of the spine.
abstract: Background Myxopapillary ependymoma (MPE) is an uncommon spinal ependymal tumor that usually arises as a solitary intradural extramedullary (IDEM) lesion in the conus medullaris, cauda equina, or filum terminale. MPE is designated WHO grade 2 since the 2021. Synchronous multifocal spinal MPE at initial presentation is rare and creates uncertainty regarding the extent and timing of surgery. Case presentation A 34-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with sudden severe non-radicular low-back pain and no neurological deficit. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and entire spine showed multiple enhancing IDEM lesions confined to the lumbosacral region (T12-L1, L2, L3-L4, L4-L5, and S1). The dominant right-sided T12-L1 lesion markedly compressed the conus medullaris/proximal cauda equina. Complete microsurgical resection of this lesion was performed, and histopathology confirmed MPE, WHO grade 2 (Ki-67 ≤ 2-3%). The patient declined radiation-oncology referral, and the remaining lesions were monitored with MRI and CSF cytology, which remained negative. Nine months later, he developed paresthesias and recurrent low-back pain, with enlargement of the L3-L4 and L4-L5 lesions. Both were completely resected in a second operation, while the stable L2 and S1 lesions were left in place. No new neurological deficit occurred after either operation. The patient subsequently underwent radiation-oncology evaluation and received radiotherapy, and the residual lesions were unchanged at 3 months. Conclusion Multifocal spinal MPE may require individualized, staged management. Prioritizing symptomatic or compressive lesions can achieve decompression and tissue diagnosis while limiting multilevel surgical morbidity. Residual disease warrants long-term imaging surveillance, CSF assessment, and evaluation for radiotherapy.

title: Preoperative endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) strain elastography for the prediction of intraoperative pancreatic texture after pancreaticoduodenectomy: a prospective diagnostic accuracy study with exploratory analysis of clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula.
abstract: Background Postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) is the most serious complication of pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD); established risk tools require intraoperative variables. We assessed the diagnostic accuracy of preoperative endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) strain elastography for intraoperative pancreatic texture and, exploratorily, predictors of clinically relevant POPF (CR-POPF). Methods Prospective single-centre study of 100 consecutive patients undergoing elective PD. The index test was preoperative EUS strain ratio (SR), threshold ≤ 2.5 prespecified before enrolment; the reference standard was intraoperative texture recorded independently by two blinded surgeons, with neck-margin fibrosis grade as secondary reference. CR-POPF (ISGPS 2016 Grade B/C) was adjudicated blind to EUS. Accuracy is reported with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs). An exploratory index used Firth-penalised regression restricted to preoperative variables, with bootstrap validation. Reporting follows STARD, TRIPOD, and STROBE. Results Soft texture occurred in 58 (58%). SR ≤ 2.5 gave 51 true positives, 7 false positives, 7 false negatives, 35 true negatives: sensitivity 87.9% (95% CI 77.1-94.0), specificity 83.3% (69.4-91.7), predictive values 87.9 and 83.3%, accuracy 86.0% (77.9-91.5), and area under the curve (AUC) 0.91 (0.84-0.96). SR rose monotonically with fibrosis grade (2.0 ± 0.6 to 5.8 ± 1.9; Spearman ρ = +0.82, p < 0.001); mean histogram elasticity fell (ρ = - 0.79, p < 0.001). CR-POPF occurred in 16 (16%). Non-PDAC pathology was unassociated with CR-POPF (9/48 vs 7/52; odds ratio 1.48, 0.51-4.35; p = 0.59). Six preoperative variables were entered simultaneously (EUS-SR, duct diameter, albumin, haemoglobin, body mass index, serum amylase; amylase carried zero points in the rounded score). Apparent AUC was 0.87 (0.79-0.94), optimism-corrected 0.78, calibration slope 0.72, and Brier score 0.096. Conclusions Preoperative EUS strain elastography at a prespecified threshold identified intraoperative pancreatic texture accurately and tracked histological fibrosis, supporting it as an objective surrogate for parenchymal consistency. The index rests on 16 events, is hypothesis-generating, and requires external multicentre validation.

title: Opportunistic PSA testing is not the safe alternative : Why Austria's non-policy on prostate cancer screening maximizes harm and forfeits the benefits.
abstract: Austria has never implemented an organized prostate cancer screening program, yet opportunistic PSA testing has been widespread for more than three decades. This has produced the harms of screening without the safeguards of a program: testing outside appropriate age and life-expectancy windows, repeated testing of low-risk men, unnecessary biopsy, overdiagnosis and overtreatment, while generating little systematic information on quality or outcomes. Randomized evidence shows that organized, repeated screening can reduce prostate cancer mortality substantially, whereas opportunistic testing delivers less benefit with more overdiagnosis. Contemporary risk-adapted pathways further improve the balance of benefit and harm: defined start and stop ages, PSA-based risk stratification, MRI before biopsy, targeted biopsy, and active surveillance can reduce unnecessary biopsies and detection or treatment of indolent disease without compromising detection of clinically significant cancer. Europe has therefore moved toward organized, PSA-based screening with MRI as a follow-up test. Austria is now participating in PRAISE-U Plus and has initiated a national multidisciplinary consensus process involving 65 experts from 22 organizations. The policy question is no longer whether Austrian men are being screened-they are-but whether screening remains unstructured or becomes organized, quality-assured and equitable. The evidence supports the latter: invite the right men, stratify risk, biopsy selectively, treat only clinically relevant disease, and measure outcomes systematically.

title: Feasibility of a lumbar CT-to-MRI image translation framework using a conditional CycleGANs for fracture stage determination in osteoporotic compression fractures.
abstract: Purpose Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides a reliable indicator of fracture stage. However, MRI scans can be expensive, time-consuming, and not readily accessible to all patients. With recent advances in artificial intelligence, translating lumbar CT images into MRI images has become feasible using cycle generative adversarial network (CycleGANs) based approaches. The aim of this study was to evaluate the feasibility of a model that translates lumbar CT images into MRI images (T1-weighted contrast-enhanced sequences) to predict the stage of osteoporotic compression fracture (OCFs) using conditional CycleGANs. Methods A total of 652 patients diagnosed with OCFs who underwent both CT and MRI within 2 weeks were retrospectively collected. Of these, 552 patients were used for training, and an independent set of 100 patients was reserved for testing. CT and MRI volumes were aligned using segmentation-based rigid registration. The proposed framework consisted of two stages: generation of vertebra-specific acute fracture maps from CT images using a 3D ResNet-based model, followed by CT-to-MRI image translation using a 3D conditional CycleGANs with acute stage conditioning. Performance was evaluated using vertebra-level classification metrics, image similarity metrics, and qualitative assessment by five experienced readers, including three spine neurosurgeons, one orthopedic spine specialist, and one radiologist. Results Fractures were most common at the thoracolumbar junction. A total of 800 vertebral bodies were analyzed. Of 678 non-acute OCFs, 667 were correctly classified and 11 were misclassified as acute; of 122 acute OCFs, 106 were correctly identified and 16 were misclassified as non-acute. Acute fracture classification achieved a precision of 0.906, recall of 0.869, and F1-score of 0.887. Synthetic MRI images showed modest quantitative agreement with real MRI (Normalized MAE 0.094 ± 0.024; PSNR 18.7 ± 1.7 dB; SSIM 0.38 ± 0.04). Qualitative evaluation demonstrated high similarity in vertebral body morphology at the fracture level, with mean similarity scores of 87.2% for the conditional CycleGAN and 85.3% for the conventional CycleGAN. Conclusions This study demonstrates the feasibility of a lumbar CT-to-MRI image translation framework using a conditional CycleGAN for determining fracture stage.
