title: Diagnostic Performance and Calibration of AI Models for Thyroid Ultrasound Malignancy Classification: From TN5000 to ThyroidXL.
abstract: We evaluated cross-dataset transportability of three frozen encoders for binary benign-versus-malignant thyroid ultrasound classification using expert-defined nodule regions and one external cohort. Logistic regression classifiers using DINOv2, TinyUSFM, and ResNet18 features were developed on 3500 TN5000 images, calibrated on 477 duplicate-clean validation images and tested on 958 images. External evaluation used maximum image scores from 2083 ThyroidXL images in 739 patients with cytological or histopathological outcomes. No external retraining, recalibration or threshold adjustment was performed. Additional analyses evaluated four classifiers, encoder-recommended preprocessing and calibration intercepts and slopes. Internal areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were 0.9081 for TinyUSFM, 0.8946 for DINOv2, and 0.8896 for ResNet18. Primary external AUROCs were 0.8464 (95% confidence interval, 0.8164-0.8731), 0.7954, and 0.7833, respectively. Sensitivities at frozen high-sensitivity thresholds were 0.9972, 0.9717, and 0.9887, but specificities were 0.1736, 0.1891, and 0.1373. External calibration intercepts were negative; slopes were 0.891, 0.645, and 0.697. DINOv2 ranked first externally with four of five classifiers. With recommended preprocessing, ResNet18 ranked first numerically (0.8329 versus 0.8214 for DINOv2); their paired difference was inconclusive. Encoder rankings depended on the classifier and preprocessing. These results apply to the three evaluated implementations, not pretraining strategies generally. Transported patient scores overestimated malignancy and had low specificity. Prospective assessment is needed before clinical use.

title: Critical Validation of Deep Learning-Based Cervical Vertebral Fracture Detection on Computed Tomography Localizer Radiographs.
abstract: Localizer radiographs are low-resolution two-dimensional overview images acquired prior to computed tomography (CT) scans. Their automated analysis could support the early detection of cervical vertebral fractures in trauma patients and thus enable immediate adjustment of imaging protocols. This study investigated to what extent deep learning-based methods can reliably detect such fractures on localizer radiographs, with a focus on critically validating model behavior beyond standard performance metrics. On a custom-annotated dataset of 346 trauma patients, two approaches were compared: a full-image binary classification and a two-step pipeline that first localizes the cervical spine and then classifies the cropped region. Model validity was assessed through a permutation test, occlusion testing, gradient-weighted class activation mapping, an analysis of potential confounders, and a subgroup analysis by anatomical fracture location. The full-image classifier formally achieved the highest test-set performance with a precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 0.477, compared with 0.349 for the cervical-spine-level classifier. Our validity analysis indicates that the full-image classifier does not primarily rely on the fracture region itself, rendering it unsuitable for clinical use. This work therefore presents a case study of shortcut learning and illustrates validation methods that may be of value for comparable studies on small datasets with visually subtle targets.

title: The Deep Learning-Based Prediction Method for Cervical Lymph Node Metastasis of Thyroid Cancer Based on Multimodal Data.
abstract: Thyroid cancer is a common malignant tumor worldwide, and there is a risk of misdiagnosis or over-treatment for small-sized thyroid cancer. The key to eliminating this risk lies in predicting cervical lymph node metastasis. The traditional manual prediction methods are not ideal, so this paper proposes an intelligent prediction method based on deep learning. This method is based on common clinical examination data, including ultrasound images, ultrasound image text descriptions, and blood test data. A deep convolutional neural network model is proposed using data from these three modalities as inputs. The model integrates multimodal data features through mean cross-attention and extracts fine-grained classification information from the fused feature map through a bilinear CNN network, demonstrating strong feature discrimination ability. Through collecting data and conducting various experiments, the experimental results show that the model proposed in this paper has good performance in predicting cervical lymph node metastasis, is better than the manual prediction, and has broad application prospects. Future research will continue to strive for data collection, increasing the amount of collected data and improving multi-center representativeness, and enhancing the diagnostic and predictive capabilities of the network model through technological improvements.

title: Learnable Pixel-Level Reward Modeling and Pixel-Wise Probability Mixing for Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation.
abstract: In semi-supervised medical image segmentation, pseudo-labeling and data mixing are widely adopted to leverage unlabeled images, yet conventional methods suffer from coarse-grained operations. Specifically, global filtering strategies typically rely on heuristic confidence scores that may not accurately reflect local pseudo-label reliability and apply spatially uniform loss weights to all pixels within retained samples, failing to reliably evaluate and accommodate spatial quality variations within pseudo-labels. Meanwhile, coarse-grained region-level mixing violently disrupts the inherent continuity of anatomical structures, frequently introducing severe semantic mismatches and misleading boundary targets during training. To address these limitations, we propose a semi-supervised segmentation framework based on learnable pixel-level reward modeling and pixel-wise probability mixing. A data-driven pixel-level reward map is constructed to provide learnable pixel-level reliability estimation instead of relying solely on heuristic confidence scores. These continuous reward scores are directly converted into fine-grained pixel-wise loss weights, dynamically regulating each pixel's optimization contribution rather than relying on hard confidence-based sample filtering; an empty-foreground safeguard only suppresses degenerate unlabeled samples with negligible predicted foreground. Furthermore, local pseudo-label distributions are adaptively refined via pixel-wise probability mixing within the continuous class probability space. This mechanism softly fuses the probability distributions of low-reward pixels with those of semantically consistent high-reward donor pixels, successfully bypassing the structural constraints of region-level mixing. Extensive experiments on the ACDC, BUSI, and Synapse datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over competitive semi-supervised baselines under limited labeled-data settings.

title: Feasibility of Simulated Low-Dose CT with Deep Learning Denoising for Lymphoma PET/CT Imaging: A Clinical Study on Lesion Detection, Staging, and Therapy Response.
abstract: [18F] FDG PET/CT is central to lymphoma staging and treatment-response assessment, but repeated examinations increase cumulative radiation exposure, largely from the CT component. This retrospective study included 152 patients with 211 whole-body PET/CT scans and evaluated whether deep learning-denoised simulated low-dose CT can preserve diagnostic performance. A single-scan cohort of 108 patients was used exclusively for model development, while an independent follow-up cohort of 44 patients (103 examinations) was reserved for quantitative evaluation and a fully crossed multi-reader, multi-case study. Simulated low-dose CT images ranging from 2/3 to 1/8 of the standard dose were reviewed, and the 1/4-dose level was selected as the lowest clinically acceptable level. A denoising model was trained using paired standard-dose CT (SDCT) and simulated low-dose CT at 1/4 of the standard dose (SLDCT) images. Six nuclear medicine physicians evaluated three imaging conditions: PET/CT with SDCT, PET/CT with SLDCT, and PET/CT with denoised SLDCT (D-SLDCT), for image quality, lesion detectability, staging, and treatment response. D-SLDCT significantly improved quantitative image quality compared with SLDCT (all p < 0.0001) and increased subjective image-quality scores (4.11 ± 0.46 vs 3.00 ± 0.00). Staging accuracy was lower under the SLDCT condition than under the SDCT condition (MAE, 1.50 ± 0.27 vs 1.40 ± 0.20; p = 0.0011), whereas the D-SLDCT condition did not differ significantly from the SDCT condition (MAE, 1.44 ± 0.22; p = 0.47). Differences were more pronounced in patients with BMI ≥ 24 kg/m 2 and among junior readers. Lesion detectability and treatment-response assessment did not differ significantly across conditions, while within-reader lesion-detection agreement with the SDCT condition improved after denoising (κ = 0.72 vs 0.67). The D-SLDCT condition preserved diagnostic performance, supporting radiation-conscious lymphoma PET/CT. This study was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR) on February 14, 2026 (registration number: ChiCTR2600119037).

title: Nondisease Sources of Radiomic Texture Variation on Plain Radiographs: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Anatomical Region, Projection, and Resolution in a Public Fracture Archive.
abstract: Radiomic texture features from plain radiographs feed machine learning models on the assumption that they reflect tissue rather than anatomy or acquisition. In a public multihospital fracture archive, we quantified how anatomical region and radiographic projection, each adjusted for the other and for image resolution, shift 17 radiomic features, how much feature variance resolution explains, and a bony superimposition contrast defined within region. This retrospective cross-sectional secondary analysis used FracAtlas (4083 musculoskeletal radiographs from three hospitals); 4024 images were analyzed. For each z-scored feature (10 first-order, 7 Gy-level co-occurrence matrix [GLCM]), linear models estimated adjusted differences (β, SD units), and resolution by variance explained (R 2 ), with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction within each factor. Superimposition (hip and shoulder vs hand and leg; n = 3630), a grouping of regions, was analyzed as a pooled regional contrast rather than an independent factor. Region shifted 16 of 17 features (radiomic uniformity, hand vs leg - 0.66 SD [95% CI - 0.72 to - 0.59]). Resolution explained up to 16.8% of single-feature variance and changed the fracture log-odds coefficient by more than 15% for 7 of 10 interpretable features. Projection had the smallest effects (radiomic 10th percentile, lateral vs frontal - 0.32 SD). The superimposition contrast produced the largest shifts (GLCM energy - 2.26 SD [95% CI - 2.36 to - 2.16]). Radiomic texture on plain radiographs varies substantially with anatomy and acquisition, independently of fracture status. Radiograph radiomics studies should record and adjust for region, projection, and resolution, report region-specific estimates, and validate across sites.

title: Panognostics-Plus: An Integrated Multi-Task AI Framework for Automated Panoramic Radiograph Interpretation with Dental Charting and Structured Reporting-Development and Technical Validation Study.
abstract: Dental charting from panoramic radiographs is essential for clinical assessment, yet remains time-consuming. This study presents Panognostics-Plus, an automated cloud-based AI framework for panoramic radiograph analysis integrating dental charting and structured radiological reporting. Panognostics-Plus was developed using a retrospective dataset of 1,595 panoramic radiographs and a YOLO-based architecture comprising modules for dental anatomy, dental treatment, and periapical diagnostics. Anatomical structures and dental treatments were analyzed using a two-stage pipeline, whereas periapical lesions were analyzed by detection-and-classification. YOLOv8m, YOLOv9m, YOLO11m, and YOLO26m were benchmarked. Detection was evaluated by precision, sensitivity, F1-score, AP, and mAP; segmentation by IoU and Dice; and processing time. Model differences were assessed using Friedman tests with Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hoc comparisons. YOLO26m achieved the highest overall performance. The largest mAP0@50:0.95 gains were observed for crowns (+ 21.3%), radicular cysts (+ 20.5%), root canal treatments (+ 17.3%), bridges (+ 14.3%), periodontal bone level (+ 14.3%), and periapical granulomas (+ 13.5%). Dental implants achieved precision, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.99, 0.98, and 0.98, respectively. Radicular cysts achieved precision, sensitivity, and F1-score of 0.95, 0.93, and 0.94 versus 0.92, 0.90, and 0.91 for periapical granulomas. Significant differences were observed in 8 of 10 detection tasks and all segmentation tasks (all p < 0.001); periodontal bone level (p = 0.193) and dental fillings (p = 0.073) were nonsignificant. Dice coefficients reached 0.97 for dental anatomy and 0.96 for dental treatments. The workflow generated a segmentation overlay, dental chart, and structured radiological report in 15 ± 1.4 s per radiograph. Panognostics-Plus may improve panoramic radiograph analysis and clinical efficiency, although further validation is required.

title: DicomDoodle: Human-in-the-Loop Annotation of 3D MRI DICOM Images with AI Support and DICOM-SEG Compatibility.
abstract: Accurate medical image annotation requires curation and remains a major bottleneck due to its time-intensive nature and inter-observer variability. To address this, we developed DicomDoodle, an open-source, Python-based tool for human-in-the-loop annotation that integrates a fine-tuned YOLO11 detector with the Segment Anything Model (SAM) 2.1 for prompt-based segmentation, alongside manual annotation and correction tools. DicomDoodle saves annotations as DICOM Segmentation (DICOM-SEG) objects, which passed automated structural conformance testing (22 checks across all 122 series) and were successfully imported and rendered in OHIF Viewer. Annotation performance was evaluated using brain MRIs from 37 patients (122 series) across three Indian hospitals, with the patient as the unit of analysis. SAM 2.1 and SAM 3 performed best among the six benchmarked SAM and MEDSAM models. Patient-level mean slice and volume IoU were poor for the fully automated workflow, at 0.109 (95% confidence interval 0.087-0.130) and 0.133 (0.102-0.164), respectively, revealing its limitations. It improved to 0.388 (0.329-0.446) and 0.338 (0.280-0.396) with slice-range prompting, and 0.858 (0.841-0.875) and 0.865 (0.843-0.886) with per-slice bounding-box prompting. For complete, unfiltered volumes, the automated workflow detected 95% of slices containing lesions. Still, it labeled about 90% of lesion-free slices as lesion-present; prompting removed almost all of these false positives. Segmentation accuracy did not degrade with lesion extent. In routine use, annotation sessions were provisionally estimated as shorter than a fixed manual reference. DicomDoodle offers an accessible, open-source platform that combines AI-assisted prompting with native DICOM-SEG generation to assist annotation.

title: Data Leakage and Unverified Provenance in Public Brain Tumor MRI Datasets: A Systematic Audit.
abstract: Brain tumor MRI classification studies routinely report accuracies above 99%, yet many public datasets in this domain trace to a few original sources and are often combined or cross-validated without accounting for shared origin. We audited seven brain tumor MRI datasets (34,525 images) for leakage within datasets and overlap between datasets typically treated as independent. Internal leakage was detected with perceptual hashing and rotation-aware structural similarity. Cross-dataset overlap was detected with ResNet-50 embedding similarity, checked against a random-pair baseline, a DenseNet-121 sensitivity analysis, and blinded two-rater review (all 75 sampled above-threshold pairs were true duplicates; 95% CI 95.1-100). A further blinded review just below the threshold found roughly half of the sampled pairs were also duplicates, so reported overlap is a lower bound. True-duplicate leakage between training and evaluation splits occurred in three of four datasets with predefined splits, including a peer-reviewed dataset and one documented as overlap-free. For 14 of 16 dataset pairs, 15.6-99.1% of the smaller dataset's images were automatically matched to the other, including datasets described as collected from named hospitals. In a controlled experiment on the one dataset with patient identifiers, image-level splitting yielded higher accuracy than patient-level splitting (97.10 ± 0.69% vs. 91.82 ± 2.77%; Welch's t-test, p = 0.017), with a 10.1-point drop in meningioma F1. This addresses within-dataset correlation only, so it is a conservative estimate of total inflation. Reported performance warrants cautious interpretation, and tooling for verifying dataset independence is lacking. We propose a checklist for dataset creators and researchers.

title: Clinical Context-Dependent Value of bpMRI-Derived Imaging Representations for Prostate Cancer Risk Stratification.
abstract: The objective was to evaluate the clinical context-dependent value of biparametric MRI (bpMRI)-derived imaging representations for prostate cancer (PCa) risk stratification, with emphasis on whether imaging features provide complementary information in patients within the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) gray zone. This dual-campus retrospective study included 536 patients with pathologically confirmed PCa who underwent pretreatment bpMRI. Patients were classified as low/intermediate and high-risk according to NCCN criteria. Patients from Campus 1 were randomly divided into training and internal test cohorts, and Campus 2 served as an independent test cohort. Radiomics, vision transformer, and contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) features were extracted from T2-weighted imaging, diffusion-weighted imaging, and apparent diffusion coefficient maps. Clinical and combined clinical-imaging models were developed. Performance was assessed using ROC analysis, calibration, decision curve analysis, and SHAP interpretation, with predefined evaluation in the PSA gray zone. In the independent test cohort, the combined model achieved the highest overall discrimination, with an AUC of 0.921, followed closely by the clinical baseline model (AUC, 0.907). Among imaging-only models, the radiomics model showed the highest overall AUC (0.844). SHAP identified PSA as the dominant predictor, indicating clinically driven overall performance. In the PSA gray zone, clinical and combined model performance declined (AUCs, 0.381 and 0.600), whereas CLIP achieved the highest AUC (0.785) and favorable net benefit. The value of bpMRI-derived imaging representations for PCa risk stratification is context-dependent. CLIP-derived representations may provide complementary discrimination when PSA-based information is less informative, supporting context-aware evaluation of imaging AI models.

title: CrossBoneNet: An Ultralightweight Hybrid CNN-ViT Architecture via Asymmetric Reversed Cross-Attention for Radiographic Fracture Detection.
abstract: Misdiagnoses in emergency departments are often associated with the difficulty in interpreting radiological findings on bone fractures due to millimetric fractures, overlapping bones, or superimpositions. Despite the high efficiency of state-of-the-art models in diagnosing such cases, their massive computational requirements severely hinder their implementation on resource-constrained devices in real-world clinical settings. In this study, we propose an ultralightweight CNN-ViT model, CrossBoneNet, which is designed for edge AI compatibility with minimal memory requirements. CrossBoneNet combines local microfracture detection using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and global anatomical recognition using vision transformers (ViTs). The model merges features from both architectures using the proposed asymmetric reversed cross-attention, where CNN features act as queries and ViT features act as keys and values-to efficiently map fine-grained local anomalies into a broader global anatomical context. Operating with a minimal parameter count (0.593 M) and low computational cost (1.527 GFLOPs), CrossBoneNet achieved a PR-AUC of 0.8498 ± 0.0086 and a ROC-AUC of 0.8427 ± 0.0072 on the MURA dataset in a patient-wise isolated evaluation. It achieves highly competitive performance-remaining within a 4% margin of the 88.59 million parameter ConvNeXt-Base model-while delivering over 99% memory savings. After fine-tuning on the FracAtlas dataset, CrossBoneNet achieved a specificity of 0.9760 ± 0.0080 and PR-AUC of 0.7568 ± 0.0414, demonstrating effective cross-domain transfer learning. With a compact footprint (< 3 MB) and high specificity at the default 0.50 operating threshold, CrossBoneNet demonstrates potential as a point-of-care decision support and worklist prioritization tool on resource-constrained devices, while calibrating the decision threshold (e.g., τ=0.3837 and τ=0.3449 ) enables high-sensitivity screening modes (achieving 85.03% and 89.96% sensitivity on MURA, respectively), pending prospective validation. This retrospective study establishes proof of concept; future work will focus on prospective clinical trials and expansion to multiclass fracture classification.

title: Conformalized Semi-Supervised Learning for Medical Imaging.
abstract: To investigate whether conformal prediction (CP)-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) can improve semi-supervised learning (SSL) frameworks. Five machine learning (ML) frameworks were developed and evaluated: supervised learning (SL), standard SSL, iterative SSL, conformalized SSL (CSSL), and iterative CSSL. Logistic regression (LR) models were trained using radiomics features extracted from MRI and CT datasets across three classification tasks: isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation prediction in gliomas, O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter methylation prediction in gliomas, and histopathological classification in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) with 95% confidence intervals, and statistical comparisons were performed using DeLong's test. Across all three tasks, uncertainty-aware SSL frameworks outperformed conventional SL and standard SSL approaches. For IDH prediction, CSSL and iterative CSSL demonstrated statistically significant improvements compared with SL and SSL (p < 0.05). For MGMT prediction, iterative SSL, CSSL, and iterative CSSL significantly outperformed SL (p < 0.05). Similarly, in NSCLC histology classification, iterative SSL and CSSL-based methods significantly improved performance compared with SL (p < 0.05). Integrating CP into SSL frameworks improves pseudo-label reliability by filtering uncertain predictions and reducing error propagation during self-training. The proposed uncertainty-aware SSL approaches demonstrated improved performance across multiple radiomics-based classification tasks, highlighting their potential utility in medical imaging applications where labeled data are limited but unlabeled data are abundant.

title: Fully Automated Segmentation of Chronic Total Occlusion Lesions on Coronary CT Angiography Using Deep Learning.
abstract: Reliable quantitative assessment for chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesions depends on accurate segmentation of coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) images. However, incomplete contrast opacification and complex lesion morphology make precise delineation particularly challenging. We developed an Atrous Attention U-Net (AAU-Net) for CTO segmentation and integrated it into a fully automated workflow comprising heart localization, CTO localization, and lesion segmentation. This retrospective study included 565 CTO lesions from 551 patients who underwent prospectively ECG-gated CCTA at three centers. Standalone segmentation used reference-mask-derived lesion-containing slices and regions of interest, whereas the automated workflow used predicted localization without reference-mask information or manual correction. Under reference-defined localization, AAU-Net achieved a Dice score of 0.8421 and intersection over union of 0.7312 in the internal test set, although performance varied by anatomical location and center. Performance decreased in the fully automated workflow, with Dice scores of 0.6922 in the internal test set, 0.5822 in external test set 1, and 0.6480 in external test set 2, potentially reflecting localization errors and differences between the separately trained segmentation models. In an exploratory locked-model radiomics analysis, features derived from automated segmentations showed numerically lower predictive performance than those derived from manual segmentations. Overall, AAU-Net showed favorable segmentation performance under reference-defined localization, but the fully automated workflow demonstrated lower performance that varied across centers. The radiomics findings demonstrate technical feasibility rather than established clinical utility. Further optimization and larger prospective multicenter validation are required before clinical deployment.

title: Tumor Semantic Modeling with Vascular Morphology Prior Correction Reduces False-Positive Malignant Predictions on Contrast-Enhanced Lung CT.
abstract: To develop an interpretable contrast-enhanced CT-based framework for benign-malignant lung tumor classification by integrating radiology-style semantic representations with global pulmonary vascular morphology features. Two particular difficulties with this task lie in (1) establishing an interpretable model to distinguish tumor data that are difficult to differentiate between benign and malignant in clinical practice, and (2) based on clinical experience, incorporate the vascular characteristics around the tumor into the decision-making process. We propose a vascular knowledge-enhanced classification framework that integrates semantic tumor representations extracted by large multimodal models with peritumoral vascular morphological features. The framework consists of three components: (1) an interpretable feature extractor for tumor representation learning, (2) vascular morphology modeling derived from vessel segmentation, and (3) a feature fusion module combining tumor and vascular information for classification. In a retrospective cohort of 420 patients with pathologically confirmed pulmonary tumors, the proposed method was assessed using patient-level, stratified five-fold cross-validation. Relative to the semantic-only branch, decision-level fusion increased accuracy (71.4% vs. 75.5%), AUC (0.764 vs. 0.816), and specificity (57.3% vs. 77.8%), but decreased sensitivity (81.1% vs. 73.9%). These findings indicate that vascular prior-guided correction primarily enhanced benign-case recognition and suppressed false-positive malignant predictions, at the expense of sensitivity for malignant cases. In single-center validation, pulmonary vascular morphology offered complementary structural evidence for differentiating benign from malignant pulmonary tumors larger than 3 cm. The proposed AND-like decision-level correction rule enhanced specificity by reducing false-positive malignant predictions.

title: ConvFormer3D: A Hybrid 3D-CNN-Transformer Front-End for Cine cMRI View Classification Pipelines.
abstract: It is vital to reliably identify the views of standard cine cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (cine cMRI), since each determines which cardiac anatomy will be observed and undergo quantitative analysis. If the view is incorrectly identified, whether by a human observer or by an automated system, errors can propagate into subsequent analyses that give rise to the volumetric assessment, strain analysis, evaluation of the valves, and thus diagnostics. Accurate classification remains a challenge due to clinical variation between scanner manufacturers, differences in acquisition protocols, and motion artifacts. This study presents ConvFormer3D, a hybrid spatiotemporal architecture that includes a Kinetics-400-pretrained 3D residual encoder (R3D-18), modified to handle single-channel cine input, combined with a lightweight temporal transformer and attention-based token pooling. The convolutional stages supply local anatomical and motion priors, while the temporal transformer captures time dependencies throughout the cardiac cycle at full temporal resolution. The network is trained using deep auxiliary supervision, label smoothing, an exponential moving average of the parameters, and mixed-precision optimization. The model's predicted probabilities are then calibrated by temperature scaling. To prevent data leakage, the different partitions are created at the level of the individual patient, and all reported metrics are recorded at patient-clustered bootstraps at the 95% confidence interval, together with formal paired significance testing between the various models. On a separate patient-level test partition, ConvFormer3D achieved an accuracy of 0.983 and an expected calibration error of 0.003 after temperature scaling.

title: Assessment of Vestibular Schwannoma Growth After Radiosurgery: Variability in Clinical Decision Thresholds and the Role of Artificial Intelligence.
abstract: Purpose To quantify expert interobserver variability in longitudinal vestibular schwannoma growth assessment after radiosurgery and evaluate AI segmentation performance relative to human variability. Materials and methods Retrospective review of patients with sporadic unilateral VS treated with stereotactic radiosurgery (2001-2023). Manual and AI segmentations were compared across the cohort. A growth-enriched subset of 24 tumors underwent additional expert assessment. Agreement was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Fleiss and Cohen κ, Bland-Altman analysis, and Dice similarity coefficients. Results The cohort included 170 MRI examinations from 85 patients (45.9% female; median age, 66 years; median follow-up, 53 months). Human interobserver agreement was excellent for baseline volume (ICC, 0.95), follow-up volume (ICC, 0.98), and percent volume change (ICC, 0.89), but decreased for ≥ 20% growth classification (Fleiss κ, 0.52). Eleven of 24 tumors met the strict-majority growth definition. AI-expert agreement was excellent for baseline and follow-up volumes (ICC, 0.99 and 0.97), but lower for percent change (ICC, 0.83). AI achieved 83.5% binary agreement (Cohen κ, 0.47) and median Dice coefficient of 0.85 (IQR, 0.77-0.90). Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a mean bias of + 6.64 percentage points (95% limits of agreement, - 53.33 to 66.60). Conclusions AI-human agreement for absolute tumor volumes was comparable to human interobserver agreement. However, longitudinal growth assessment and binary classification demonstrated greater variability, emphasizing the importance of benchmarking AI performance against human variability when applying clinically relevant growth thresholds.

Results

The cohort included 170 MRI examinations from 85 patients (45.9% female; median age, 66 years; median follow-up, 53 months). Human interobserver agreement was excellent for baseline volume (ICC, 0.95), follow-up volume (ICC, 0.98), and percent volume change (ICC, 0.89), but decreased for ≥ 20% growth classification (Fleiss κ, 0.52). Eleven of 24 tumors met the strict-majority growth definition. AI-expert agreement was excellent for baseline and follow-up volumes (ICC, 0.99 and 0.97), but lower for percent change (ICC, 0.83). AI achieved 83.5% binary agreement (Cohen κ, 0.47) and median Dice coefficient of 0.85 (IQR, 0.77-0.90). Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a mean bias of + 6.64 percentage points (95% limits of agreement, - 53.33 to 66.60).

Conclusions

AI-human agreement for absolute tumor volumes was comparable to human interobserver agreement. However, longitudinal growth assessment and binary classification demonstrated greater variability, emphasizing the importance of benchmarking AI performance against human variability when applying clinically relevant growth thresholds.

title: Physics-Informed Implicit Neural Networks for 3D Coronary Artery Reconstruction.
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of coronary artery geometry from computed tomography angiography (CCTA)-derived segmentations is challenging because of thin vessel walls, tortuous trajectories, and small distal structures. We propose a physics-informed implicit neural network (PIINN) for case-specific reconstruction of paired coronary surfaces from pre-segmented CCTA-derived lumen and outer-wall geometries. For each coronary segment, a single network is optimized independently to represent the luminal and outer vessel-wall surfaces using dual signed distance fields (SDFs). The objective combines supervised SDF regression and boundary anchoring with Eikonal regularization and geometry- and anatomy-informed soft constraints on surface ordering, enclosure consistency, and local wall separation. A three-stage curriculum progressively adjusts the spatial sampling, learning rate, and constraint weights. The framework was evaluated on 15 coronary artery segments. The PIINN (256 × 6) achieved a near-surface RMSE of 0.26 mm and a sign accuracy approaching 90% for the outer SDF. Mesh reconstruction achieved an inner-surface ASSD of 0.166 mm and an HD95 of 0.455 mm, compared with the ASSD values of 0.290 mm for Vanilla INR and 1.057 mm for DeepSDF, with statistically significant improvements across the evaluated cases (p ≤ 0.003). Component-wise ablation further demonstrated distinct contributions from Eikonal regularization, anatomical constraints, region-based sampling, and curriculum optimization. These results support PIINN as a constrained continuous representation for case-specific coronary reconstruction from CCTA-derived segmentations; direct reconstruction from raw CCTA and generalization to unseen patients were not evaluated.

title: Unleashing the potential of saturation-transfer MR fingerprinting (ST-MRF) in neuro-oncology: quantitative molecular CEST and MTC mapping.
abstract: Neuro-oncology biomarkers allow probing tissues beyond anatomical or relaxation contrast. However, new techniques are needed to achieve mechanistic elucidation and effective therapeutic interventions. Quantitative MRI techniques, such as T 1 , T 2 , diffusion, and perfusion imaging, provide insights into tumor biology, infiltration, microstructure, and hemodynamics, and have been implemented clinically, but are limited in probing cellular and molecular changes. Saturation transfer (ST) MRI methods, including magnetization transfer contrast (MTC) and chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST), exhibit enhanced sensitivity to semisolid macromolecular content, mobile proteins, tissue metabolites, and acidosis. Despite these advantages, ST-MRI techniques typically have been qualitative or semi-quantitative, time-consuming, and impractical for clinical implementation. However, emerging ST-MR fingerprinting (ST-MRF) represents a significant analytical advancement by integrating RF saturation preparation into a pseudo-randomized MRF acquisition framework with a deep learning-based reconstruction. This approach enables simultaneous, clinically realistic, quantitative mapping of bulk water relaxation properties (e.g., T 1 and T 2 ), semisolid macromolecular parameters, and exchangeable solute dynamics (e.g., pool size ratios and exchange rates). We provide a comprehensive background, methodological principles, and evolving clinical applications of ST-MRF in neuro-oncology. We explore current advancements, strengths, limitations, and future possibilities for clinical translation into neuro-oncology workflows, including tumor characterization, treatment response monitoring, infiltration mapping, and biomarker development.

title: MORSE-PI: flexible and artefact-free image reconstruction for structural and functional QSM and other phase-critical imaging applications.
abstract: Purpose Phase imaging applications such as QSM are highly sensitive to noise amplifications, phase singularities, and other artefacts, particularly in challenging scenarios such as ultra-high field (7 T), under-sampled or single-echo acquisitions. We present a novel image reconstruction method, MORSE-PI, designed to produce high-SNR, artefact-free, and singularity-free phase images for both structural (SWI, QSM) and functional (fQSM) phase-based brain imaging. Methods MORSE-PI extends our previous approach, MORSE, by introducing a Virtual Reference Coil (VRC). The VRC is constructed as a linear combination of coil sensitivity maps, with correlations enhanced between coil elements using the noise covariance matrix. Such a VRC ensures robust signal support across the entire brain and is used to correct phase offsets in the MORSE-derived coil sensitivity estimates, resulting in artefact-free, high-SNR phase. Results Compared to GRAPPA with ASPIRE phase correction, MORSE-PI demonstrates greater robustness to artefacts such as noise amplification and aliasing, and shows improved reproducibility in structural imaging at both 3 T and 7 T. Unlike ESPIRiT and GRAPPA combined with adaptive coil combination methods, MORSE-PI yields singularity-free phase maps. MORSE-PI enables high-SNR reconstructions even for the most challenging scenarios, such as single-echo EPI at 7 T. Its efficient, containerised implementation using the Gadgetron framework supports deployment on the MRI scanner console during measurements. Conclusion MORSE-PI offers a flexible and computationally efficient solution for generating high-SNR, artefact- and singularity-free phase images in both single- and multi-echo GRE and EPI acquisitions. This makes it particularly well-suited for structural and functional QSM, as well as other phase-based MRI applications. Its robustness and rapid computational time facilitate efficient deployment on scanners across field strengths.

title: Observer agreement in sonographic glandular tissue component classification and sonographic breast density assessment: a multi-institutional study.
abstract: Purpose The sonographic glandular tissue component (GTC) is a potential imaging biomarker for stratifying breast cancer risk in women with dense breasts. This study evaluated the reproducibility, reliability, and clinical applicability of GTC classification and GTC-based sonographic breast density assessment in a multicenter observer study. Methods Fifteen readers (nine physicians and six sonographers) from 12 institutions independently assessed 100 paired ultrasound images twice, 1 month apart, with the dataset rearranged for the second reading. GTC was qualitatively classified into four categories according to its estimated proportion within the fibroglandular tissue (FGT): minimal, mild, moderate, and marked; minimal/mild were grouped as low GTC and moderate/marked as high GTC. Sonographic breast density was categorized as sonographic dense breast (high GTC), sonographic non-dense breast (visible fat lobules), or intermediate, with intermediate cases further divided into high or low categories using an FGT-to-FAT (subcutaneous and retromammary fat) ratio cutoff of 1. Interobserver and intraobserver agreement was evaluated using κ statistics. Results Substantial interobserver agreement was observed for the four-class GTC classification, the two-class GTC classification, and sonographic breast density assessment. Intraobserver agreement was moderate for the four-class GTC classification and substantial for the two-class GTC classification and sonographic breast density assessment. The majority-vote sonographic breast density assessment showed substantial agreement with the mammographic ground truth, whereas individual-reader assessments showed moderate concordance with mammographic breast density both overall and in intermediate-density breasts. No significant differences in agreement were observed between physicians and sonographers. Conclusion Substantial interobserver agreement and moderate-to-substantial intraobserver agreement support the reproducibility and reliability of GTC classification and GTC-based sonographic breast density assessment.

title: Spatially Resolved 3D Mechanobiological Model of Rat Femoral Fracture Healing Integrating Mechanics, Vasculature, and Cell Migration.
abstract: Fracture repair arises from the interaction of mechanical, vascular, and cellular processes whose spatial organization remains difficult to predict. We developed an image-derived three-dimensional mechanobiological framework that couples finite-element mechanics, strain-regulated vascularization, progenitor-cell redistribution, and tissue differentiation within a controlled rat femoral osteotomy-and-fixation construct. Model outputs were compared regionally and temporally with ex vivo micro-computed tomography (μCT) and histology over a 6-week healing period. The simulation reproduced several experimentally observed spatial features, including early peripheral/periosteal mineralization followed by later fracture-centered consolidation. Using a calibration/evaluation framework in which day 35 was used to map simulated regional stiffness to μCT bone area and days 14, 21, 28, and 42 were withheld for evaluation, the combined migration formulation showed the strongest overall held-out model-experiment correspondence (Pearson r = 0.57, Spearman ρ = 0.78, MAE = 0.70 mm 2 , RMSE = 0.88 mm 2 , R 2 = 0.30). Correspondence was weaker for diffusion-only, mechanically guided only, and no migration control. Thus, the migration formulation influenced downstream predictions of regional mineralization, with the combined diffusion and mechanical-guidance formulation showing the strongest correspondence with held-out μCT measurements, although substantial regional error and imperfect absolute calibration remained. Data-driven analysis of simulated element-wise stiffness trajectories identified reproducible computational trajectory classes that exhibited distinct anatomical distributions. Early simulated mechanobiological features were also associated with later simulated stiffness; because this analysis operates entirely within the simulation, it characterizes internal predictive structure rather than independent biological outcome prediction. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of coupling image-derived 3D geometry, mechanics, vascularization, and progenitor cell migration to study spatial heterogeneity during fracture repair in a single, well-controlled construct. Validation across additional geometries, fixation environments, and independent experimental datasets is required before broader biological or clinical generalization.

title: Agreement between fully automated artificial intelligence and cardiac radiologists for coronary stenosis and plaque assessment in an asymptomatic screening cohort.
abstract: This retrospective single-center study evaluated segment-level agreement between experienced cardiac radiologists and a research AI platform for coronary stenosis and plaque assessment on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA). Asymptomatic individuals undergoing CCTA at a health screening center were studied, excluding those with prior revascularization, coronary anomaly, or total occlusion. Stenosis grade and plaque composition were independently assessed by the AI platform and two cardiac radiologists at the segment level, with disagreements between the two radiologists resolved by consensus. Agreement was evaluated using Cohen's κ, quadratic weighted κ for ordinal grading, observed agreement, and positive and negative agreement for dichotomized significant stenosis. The cohort comprised 172 participants and 2,582 segments. Significant stenosis was uncommon (18/2,582, 0.7%), with moderate agreement (κ = 0.412; observed agreement 98.5%; positive agreement 0.418; negative agreement 0.992). Agreement was fair for ordinal stenosis grade (κ = 0.397; quadratic weighted κ = 0.573; observed agreement 84.0%) and plaque composition (κ = 0.330; observed agreement 81.8%). Stenosis-grade agreement was lower in plaque-containing than plaque-free segments, an exploratory finding given marked differences in subgroup size and prevalence. Myocardial bridging and image quality were not major descriptive determinants of discordance. In this low-prevalence cohort, AI-based CCTA analysis showed high negative agreement for radiologist-defined significant stenosis but limited concordance for grading and plaque characterization. Reflecting low prevalence and few positive cases, the findings do not establish independent rule-out performance but support prospective evaluation of AI as an expert-supervised pre-reading or triage adjunct, with positive, ambiguous, or plaque-containing findings requiring expert review.

title: Accelerated aortic stenosis progression is associated with greater CT-derived extracellular volume.
abstract: Rapid progression of aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with adverse outcomes, yet the myocardial changes accompanying faster progression remain incompletely characterized. We evaluated the association between the rate of AS progression and myocardial fibrosis assessed by computed tomography (CT)-derived extracellular volume fraction (ECV), and the impact on clinical outcomes. We studied 134 patients with classical high-gradient severe AS who underwent pre-transcatheter aortic valve implantation cardiac CT with a delayed dual-energy acquisition for ECV quantification and had at least two echocardiograms ≥ 6 months apart. Progression was defined as the annualized change in peak aortic jet velocity. Rapid progression was defined as an increase > 0.30 m/s/year. Patients were followed for a composite of cardiovascular hospitalization, urgent aortic valve replacement, or death. ECV correlated with progression rate (Spearman ρ = 0.33, p < 0.001). In multivariable linear regression, faster progression remained independently associated with ECV (β = 2.52, p = 0.001). Rapid progressors had higher ECV than slow progressors (31.5% vs. 28.3%, p < 0.001). Over a median follow-up of 16.2 months, 36 patients (26.9%) reached the composite outcome. Patients with both rapid progression and high ECV had an event rate of 69 versus 11 per 100 patient-years in those without (adjusted HR 6.22, 95% CI 3.13-12.32). Faster AS progression is independently associated with greater diffuse myocardial fibrosis, irrespective of stenosis severity, and their combination identified patients at higher risk of adverse events. These findings suggest that AS progression rate and myocardial tissue characterization carry complementary prognostic information in severe AS.

title: Transmitral flow analysis via valve tracking 4D flow MRI detects age- and sex-related diastolic changes.
abstract: To evaluate whether valve tracking 4D flow MRI can detect subtle age- and sex-related changes in left ventricular (LV) diastolic function in healthy adults. We retrospectively recruited healthy adults who had undergone cardiac MRI between October 2020 and March 2022, selecting those with whole-heart 4D flow MRI, 2D long-axis cine, and short-axis cine acquisitions. A dynamic plane at the mitral valve (MV) level was generated in 4D flow MRI using leaflet insertion points tracked on 2- and 4-chamber cine images. Through-plane velocities were computed from 4D flow data and corrected for MV motion. After contouring the transmitral region, early and late diastolic peak flow rates (E flow , A flow ), peak velocities (E vel, A vel ), and mitral forward flow volume (MFVol) were measured. Peak early LV relaxation velocity (E MV ) was defined as the peak through-plane velocity of MV plane motion. A total of 39 adults (age range: 46 ± 13; 20 women) were included. With age, both E flow /A flow (r = - 0.79, p < 0.0001, adjusted for HR) and E vel /A vel (r = - 0.70, p < 0.0001, adjusted for HR) were significantly decreased, while E vel /E MV increased (r = 0.53, p < 0.001, adjusted for EDV). Early diastolic changes were sex-specific; women showed decreased E flow and increased E vel /E MV with aging, whereas men showed no significant associations. Additionally, the normalized E flow /MFVol decreased with aging, significantly in the sex-combined cohort (r = - 0.42, p = 0.008) and in women (r = - 0.68, p = 0.004), but not in men. Transmitral flow rates and peak velocities assessed by 4D flow MRI with cine-based valve tracking effectively detected physiologic age-related declines in diastolic function, exhibiting sex-specific differences.

title: Progress in multimodal imaging assessment of the correlation between perivascular adipose tissue and atherosclerosis.
abstract: Cardiovascular disease remains a leading cause of death and disability worldwide. Adipose tissue dysfunction is a key driver, and perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) exerts location‑specific effects on the cardiovascular system. This review focuses on PVAT in atherosclerosis, with particular attention to pericoronary PVAT, epicardial adipose tissue (EAT), carotid PVAT, and peri-aortic adipose tissue (PAAT). PVAT homeostasis relies on UCP1‑mediated thermogenesis for metabolic modulation and on paracrine signaling via adiponectin and apelin. Under aging, obesity, or diabetes, PVAT switches from an anti‑inflammatory to a pro‑inflammatory phenotype, accelerating plaque formation through bidirectional inflammatory crosstalk. For clinical assessment, this review highlights progress in multimodal imaging technologies, including CT fat attenuation index, MRI water‑lipid separation, PET/CT, and echocardiography, for noninvasive quantification of PVAT density, composition, and metabolic activity, and compares their advantages and limitations. This review further discusses artificial intelligence (AI)-driven radiomic and radiotranscriptomic approaches that extend PVAT assessment beyond conventional single-parameter metrics. We systematically review the research progress of these techniques in evaluating dynamic PVAT changes and their correlation with atherosclerosis, aiming to clarify the intrinsic correlation between imaging‑derived PVAT functional status and AS development.

title: Preoperative classification of histopathological growth patterns in colorectal liver metastases using prospective 18 F-FDG PET/CT.
abstract: Colorectal liver metastases (CLM) exhibit distinct histopathological growth patterns (HGPs) at the metastasis-liver interface, clinically relevant for prognosis and potential predictive value. This study investigates the feasibility of using Fluorine-18 Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography Computed Tomography ( 18 F-FDG PET/CT) to preoperatively classify HGPs in CLM and secondly investigate PET parameters as prognostic markers for overall survival (OS). In a prospective study at Umeå University Hospital (June 2013-December 2017), 78 patients with resectable CLM underwent contrast-enhanced liver MRI and 18 F-FDG PET/CT imaging. HGP classification was performed on tissue sections according to 2017 international guidelines. PET features (SUV mean [standardised uptake value], SUV max , metabolic tumour volume [MTV] and first-order texture metrics) were analysed to distinguish encapsulating (eHGP) from replacement (rHGP) patterns. In pretreated patients, multivariate logistic regression including both metabolic and texture parameters identified significant associations for parameters from the fixed level threshold algorithm (VuePoint Sharp IR) with small odds ratios. Overall, PET parameters showed limited ability to discriminate between eHGP and rHGP. OS was superior with eHGP versus rHGP (log-rank p = 0.045). In chemonaïve patients, SUV-based metrics showed unadjusted exploratory associations with OS after liver surgery, varying by reconstruction/delineation and were not significant after correction for multiple testing. FDG-PET-derived parameters were not reliably associated with HGP and did not support non-invasive HGP prediction in this cohort. eHGP was associated with superior survival, underscoring the value of HGP assessment for prognostication while alternative non-invasive biomarkers remain to be identified.

title: Baseline OCT Biomarkers Associated with Anatomical Response and Long-Term Reinjection Burden in Diabetic Macular Edema Treated with Intravitreal Dexamethasone Implant.
abstract: Purpose To identify baseline optical coherence tomography (OCT) biomarkers associated with 6 month anatomical response and 36 month reinjection burden in anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF)-pretreated eyes with diabetic macular edema (DME) switched to dexamethasone (DEX) implant. Methods This retrospective single-center cohort included 130 eyes (130 patients) followed for 36 months. Good 6 month anatomical response was defined as a ≥ 20% reduction in central subfield thickness (CST) with complete resolution of intraretinal and subretinal fluid, and frequent reinjection as ≥ 5 DEX implants within 36 months. Multivariable logistic regression was used (Firth penalized regression for reinjection), with a CST-independent fluid-resolution endpoint used as sensitivity analysis. Results Sixty eyes (46.2%) achieved good anatomical response. Hyperreflective foci (HRF; OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02-0.48), disorganization of the retinal inner layers (DRIL; OR 0.16, 0.05-0.47), and external limiting membrane (ELM) disruption (OR 0.16, 0.04-0.54) were independently associated with lower odds of response (optimism-corrected AUC 0.88) and remained significant for fluid resolution. Seventy-nine eyes (60.8%) received ≥ 5 implants. Ellipsoid zone (EZ) disruption (OR 24.83, 3.73-345.08) and DRIL (OR 5.03, 1.45-20.27) were independently associated with frequent reinjection (optimism-corrected AUC 0.95). Month-6 and month-36 anatomical status agreed in 85.4% of eyes. Intraocular pressure > 25 mmHg occurred in 26.2% of eyes, all controlled medically. Conclusion Baseline OCT biomarkers were associated with both early anatomical response and long-term reinjection burden after switching to DEX. HRF, DRIL, and ELM disruption were associated with a lower likelihood of 6 month response, whereas EZ disruption and DRIL were associated with a higher 36 month reinjection burden. These prognostic associations require external validation.

Month-6 and month-36 anatomical status agreed in 85.4% of eyes. Intraocular pressure > 25 mmHg occurred in 26.2% of eyes, all controlled medically.

Conclusion

Baseline OCT biomarkers were associated with both early anatomical response and long-term reinjection burden after switching to DEX. HRF, DRIL, and ELM disruption were associated with a lower likelihood of 6 month response, whereas EZ disruption and DRIL were associated with a higher 36 month reinjection burden. These prognostic associations require external validation.

title: Mapping Research on AI-Based Computer-Aided Diagnosis and Clinical Decision Support Systems: a Bibliometric Study Integrating Google Trends and Content Analysis.
abstract: Research on artificial intelligence-based computer-aided diagnosis and clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) is expanding, but integrated evidence on publication patterns, keyword trajectories, online search activity, and methodological characteristics remains limited. To characterize AI-CDSS research by integrating bibliometric analysis, Google Trends comparison, and structured content analysis of citation-ranked publications. Scholarly interest was assessed using bibliometric analysis of Web of Science records from 2016 through August 2026, including author-keyword co-occurrence, bibliographic coupling, and reference co-citation, whereas Google Trends was used to characterize online search activity. A structured content analysis of citation-ranked publications was conducted to examine applications, methodological characteristics, and reported limitations. We analyzed 19,809 included publications from 2016 through August 2026. Output rose approximately 21-fold, from 193 records in 2016 to 4,082 in 2025. Output was geographically concentrated within the included corpus, with a Gini coefficient of 0.869. Among records with identifiable corresponding-author country or territory, China, the United States, and India accounted for 61.33%. Scientific Reports was the most frequent source (n = 916). Frequent artificial intelligence- and diagnosis-related keywords included machine learning (n = 5,666), deep learning (n = 4,022), and computer-aided diagnosis (n = 1,512). Bibliographic coupling identified 15 publication communities, and reference co-citation identified seven reference communities. In the monthly level-series comparison, 9 of 10 keyword concepts exhibited significant associations with Google Trends relative search interest, but none of the 10 first-difference associations remained significant after Bonferroni adjustment. Content analysis of 215 citation-ranked publications, including 191 empirical publications, showed frequent use of convolutional neural networks in diagnostic and radiology applications. Common limitations included limited external validation, infrequent calibration reporting, and sparse workflow-level or impact evaluation. AI-CDSS research has rapidly expanded around machine learning, deep learning, and diagnostic applications, but the analyzed citation-ranked publications provide more evidence of methodological development than of clinical deployment. Integrating bibliometric, search-activity, and content-based perspectives shows limited short-term correspondence between online search activity and scholarly keyword use and highlights the need to move beyond model development toward independent external validation, prospective workflow and patient-outcome evaluation, calibration, fairness, and postdeployment monitoring.

title: Explainable machine learning predictive models for treatment response after SBRT in melanoma brain metastases.
abstract: Purpose/objective To develop an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model to predict the complete/partial response of oligometastatic brain lesions from melanoma (MBMs) two months after from radiosurgical or fractionated stereotactic treatments. Material/methods 50 consecutive patients with a total 102 MBMs treated with CyberKnife® SBRT from December 2012 to December 2018 were selected within the Rabbit study. Local response was evaluated on brain MRI performed during follow-up using response evaluation criteria in solid tumors (RECIST) and revised using response criteria for brain metastases from the response assessment in neuro-oncology criteria (RANO) group. For each treated lesion, the following variables were considered: number of treated lesions, the LDH pre-treatment level, previous treatments (surgery or whole brain RT), BRAF status, time from primary diagnosis to brain lesions discovery (Time_diag), lesion dimensions and site, SBRT dose and fractionation, type of concomitant treatment with ipilimumab (IPI). Six different supervised machine learning models, including logistic regression (LR), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), decision tree (DT) and light gradient boosting (LGBM), were trained and internally validated with 5-fold cross validation. Model performances were assessed using receiving operator curves (ROC) and area under the curve (AUC). An explainable approach based on SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method was deployed to generate individual explanations of the model decisions. Lastly, a decision tree was created to better understand and interpret the complex relationships between the covariates and the target variable. Results 23.5% of lesions had a complete or partial response and were used as ground truth for the ML models. The best performing model was the LGBM, reporting a mean AUCs in the 5-fold cross validation of 0.87 (0.85-0.91). SHAP analysis strongly associated complete/partial response with four variables, namely in order of importance: the BRAF status, the total dose, the type of treatment with ipilimumab, and the lesion dimension. In particular, the DT classified patients with BRAF "wild-type" status having only 10.7% probability to reach complete/partial response. Among these lesions, those treated with doses < 24 Gy had 0% probability of complete/partial response. By contrast, lesions with a BRAF "mutated" status reported a probability of complete/partial response of 39.1%. Among these lesions, those treated with concomitant ipilimumab reached 100% probability of complete/partial response. Conclusion Machine-learning models enable a reliable prediction of the treatment response of oligometastatic lesions receiving SBRT. This approach may assist radiation oncologists to tailor more individualized treatment plans in this clinical setting. An external validation of the results is mandatory.

title: Lateral and suprasellar MRI anatomy in pituitary neuroendocrine tumor surgery: interobserver agreement and associations with resection and intraoperative CSF leakage.
abstract: Purpose Lateral cavernous-sinus extension and suprasellar tumor-arachnoid anatomy are distinct but overlapping dimensions of pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (PitNET) surgery. We evaluated whether reader-concordant preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) descriptors of these two axes show different associations with extent of resection and intraoperative cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage. Methods In this single-center retrospective study, two blinded neurosurgeons independently assessed preoperative MRI of 53 patients: modified Knosp grade, suprasellar height, bowing index, infundibular deviation angle, and a study-specific tumor-arachnoid cleft grade. Exploratory analyses examined resection extent and Esposito-graded leakage (15 events), with post hoc adjustment for maximal tumor diameter. Results Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) were 0.995-0.999 for continuous measures; cleft agreement was 53/53 and Knosp exact agreement 96.2%. Knosp grade was most strongly associated with non-total resection (area under the curve [AUC] 0.908; diameter-adjusted odds ratio [OR] 10.8 per SD, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.4-48.9) but not leakage (AUC 0.648). Suprasellar height (AUC 0.747) and cleft grade (AUC 0.740) showed stronger leakage associations; none of 16 patients with a wide cleft (> 2 mm) leaked. Cleft grade and height were strongly collinear (ρ=-0.81); the cleft-leakage association persisted after diameter adjustment (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.19-0.93). Conclusion Lateral and suprasellar MRI descriptors, concordant between two readers, showed different, partly overlapping operative associations. Modified Knosp grade related most strongly to resection, whereas suprasellar features, particularly the study-specific cleft grade, showed stronger exploratory associations with intraoperative leakage. The cleft finding is hypothesis-generating and requires prospective external validation; added value over height and the sellar barrier is unproven.

title: Diffusion anisotropy as an imaging biomarker of directional progression in temporal glioblastoma.
abstract: Purpose Glioblastoma frequently progresses beyond surgical margins, yet whether preoperative imaging can predict its direction remains unclear. Given the anatomical characteristics of the temporal lobe and the potential role of anterior temporal lobectomy, we evaluated FLAIR, isotropic diffusion (DTI-p), and diffusion anisotropy (DTI-q) as imaging biomarkers of directional progression after complete resection. Materials and methods We retrospectively analyzed a prospectively recruited multicenter cohort of patients with newly diagnosed IDH-wildtype glioblastoma confined to the temporal lobe who underwent complete resection of contrast-enhancing tumor and had preoperative diffusion tensor imaging and follow-up MRI demonstrating progression. Progression was visually classified relative to the resection cavity. Direction-specific accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were calculated, with paired comparisons using exact McNemar tests and Holm correction across all comparisons. Times to progression and death were summarized descriptively. Results Thirty-two patients met inclusion criteria. DTI-q demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy across all progression directions (median, 75%), compared with DTI-p (median, 50%) and FLAIR (median, 44%). DTI-q significantly outperformed FLAIR and DTI-p for lateral, superior, and inferior progression after Holm correction. Combined imaging models did not improve predictive performance over DTI-q alone. Conclusion Preoperative DTI-q predicted directional progression after complete resection more accurately than FLAIR or DTI-p, supporting DTI-q as a potential imaging biomarker for spatially informed surgical planning.

title: Hypoxia-powered MRI guides supramaximal biosurgical sampling of glioblastoma infiltration: the GLIOXY initiative.
abstract: Purpose To assess the feasibility of using hypoxia-powered magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to guide prospective sampling of high-response habitats beyond contrast enhancement in glioblastoma. Methods Nine treatment-naive patients with histologically confirmed isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wildtype glioblastoma underwent blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) MRI during a controlled transient hypoxic stimulus on the evening before surgery. Anatomical segmentation and voxel-wise temporal decomposition generated normalized hypoxia response maps. Otsu thresholding defined a high-response habitat outside contrast enhancement. Targets were confirmed with the surgeon according to anatomical accessibility and eloquence, transferred to neuronavigation, and sampled before major debulking. We divided the specimen for formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded neuropathology and frozen-tissue storage. Results Neuronavigation transfer succeeded in all nine cases. Eight targets were accessible and sampled. Seven sampled targets contained tumor. One yielded reactive cortex and white matter without definite tumor. No target-sampling complications were observed among the eight sampled procedures. Conclusion Hypoxia-powered MRI could be integrated into prospective neuronavigation-guided sampling beyond contrast enhancement. Tumor was identified in seven of eight sampled targets. By translating a tracer-free physiological response map into coordinate-matched tissue, the GLIOXY workflow enables prospective, targeted tissue sampling of non-enhancing glioblastoma regions.

title: Serial serum lactate dehydrogenase dynamics as an adjunctive biomarker for differentiating true progression from treatment-related changes in IDH-wild-type glioblastoma.
abstract: Background Differentiating true tumor progression from pseudoprogression and radiation necrosis remains a major clinical challenge in patients with IDH-wild-type glioblastoma after radiotherapy and temozolomide. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is inexpensive, widely available and repeatable, but it is a nonspecific systemic marker whose tissue source cannot be inferred from total serum activity. We therefore evaluated serial LDH dynamics as an adjunctive, hypothesis-generating biomarker rather than as a glioblastoma-specific tumor marker. Methods We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients treated at a single tertiary neuro-oncology center with histologically confirmed IDH-wild-type glioblastoma who developed new or increasing contrast enhancement after standard radiochemotherapy and had available serum LDH measurements at baseline and at the time of suspicious MRI. Final diagnosis was assigned using histology when available or a composite reference standard based on multidisciplinary review and longitudinal imaging follow-up. LDH at suspicious MRI and LDH percentage change from baseline were evaluated for their ability to distinguish true progression from treatment-related changes. Results The cohort included 180 patients: 101 with true progression and 79 with treatment-related changes, including 65 pseudoprogression and 14 radiation necrosis cases. Median LDH at suspicious MRI was higher in true progression than in treatment-related changes (371 vs 273 U/L), as was median LDH percentage increase from baseline (28.7% vs 5.8%). Baseline LDH showed limited discrimination (AUC 0.675), whereas event LDH and LDH percentage change showed stronger performance (AUC 0.855 and 0.872, respectively). An exploratory LDH signature, defined as event LDH ≥ 293 U/L or LDH increase ≥ 25%, showed high sensitivity (95.0%) and negative predictive value (90.0%) but moderate specificity (57.0%). Conclusions In this single-center retrospective cohort, serial total-serum LDH dynamics were associated with final diagnostic classification after suspicious post-treatment MRI in IDH-wild-type glioblastoma. Because serum LDH is biologically nonspecific and the present study did not determine LDH isoenzymes or cellular origin, LDH should not be interpreted as a glioma-specific tumor marker or used as a stand-alone test. Its potential role is limited to an adjunctive signal within a multimodal RANO-informed diagnostic framework, and prospective external validation with source-resolved LDH analyses is required.

title: MRI-defined necrosis morphology, circulating immune profiles and survival in glioblastoma.
abstract: Purpose Necrosis is a defining feature and an active hypoxic niche implicated in immune escape and treatment resistance in glioblastoma (GBM). We asked whether MRI-defined necrosis morphology is associated with circulating immune profiles and overall survival (OS). Methods We retrospectively studied 111 patients with newly diagnosed IDH-wildtype GBM resected in 2018-2024. Preoperative necrosis was classified visually as classic confluent or multiloculated. Two blinded readers reclassified all cases independently. Immune subsets were assessed by flow cytometry (n = 59, 48/11 classic/multiloculated) and plasma cytokines by multiplex immunoassay (n = 54, 45/9). All 28 immune analytes were exploratory, corrected across the panel. OS from surgery was analyzed with Kaplan-Meier and Cox models, including treatment and small-sample sensitivity analyses. Results Inter-reader agreement was kappa = 0.883. Multiloculated morphology was associated with longer OS (median, 17.4 vs. 14.4 months; HR, 0.55, 95% CI, 0.31-0.98, p = 0.041), including after multivariable adjustment (n = 94; HR, 0.42, 0.22-0.81, p = 0.010; Firth-penalized, 0.44, p = 0.007), exclusion of untreated patients and early deaths, and restriction to completed chemoradiation (HR, 0.37, 0.16-0.84, p = 0.018). Classic morphology was associated with fewer conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) (0.15% vs. 0.41%, p = 0.006), more mature natural killer cells (p = 0.022), and lower granzyme B, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, and IL-10, but no difference survived correction (lowest q = 0.088). Multiloculated patients were younger (57.2 vs. 64.3 years, p = 0.032). The cDC association did not persist after adjustment for deep-seated location (p = 0.124). Conclusions Multiloculated necrosis was associated with longer OS after adjustment for established prognostic factors, which requires external validation. Circulating immune differences were exploratory and could not be separated from tumor location. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Molecular Imaging of Liver Fibrosis using [<sup>68</sup>Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT: A Prospective head-to-head comparison with Transient Elastography, Serum Biomarkers & Metavir Histopathological Staging.
abstract: Chronic liver disease (CLD) leading to cirrhosis is a major cause of global morbidity and mortality. Histopathological evaluation by liver biopsy remains the gold standard for fibrosis staging, but its invasive nature limits routine use. Non-invasive tools such as serum biomarkers and transient elastography (TE) are widely used but they have recognised limitations. This prospective study performed a comprehensive head-to-head comparison of [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT uptake with serum fibrosis scores, TE, and histopathology across all stages of liver fibrosis in a well-characterised CLD cohort. Materials and methods Fifty-four patients with CLD of different etiologies (51.9% non-alcoholic fatty liver disease [NAFLD], 29.6% viral hepatitis, 11.1% autoimmune hepatitis) underwent [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT together with clinical and biochemical evaluation. Serum fibrosis markers (APRI, FIB-4, and NFS) were calculated, and TE was performed in 52 patients. Liver biopsy (n = 22) was obtained when clinically indicated, or in cases of discordance between non-invasive tests. Hepatic tracer uptake was quantified employing two methodologies (a) a four-region-of-interest (4-ROI) approach as well as (b) whole-liver segmentation approach. Correlations between FAPI uptake and fibrosis markers were assessed using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis determined diagnostic performance for clinically significant fibrosis (≥ F2) and cirrhosis (F4). Patients with discrepant results underwent systematic re-evaluation with repeat TE and/or histopathology to establish a conclusive diagnosis. Additionally, an agreement analysis between the 4-ROI method and whole-liver segmentation was assessed for background-corrected SUVmean using Bland-Altman analysis. The strength of agreement was quantified using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC). Results Hepatic [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 uptake increased progressively with advancing fibrosis, being visually evident in advanced stages (F3-F4) and rising in parallel with liver stiffness measurement (LSM). Uptake correlated moderately with LSM, APRI, and FIB-4. For clinically significant fibrosis (≥ F2), an average SUVmean threshold (4-ROI) of 0.76 yielded 86.0% sensitivity and 88.9% specificity (AUC 0.88). For cirrhosis (F4), an average SUVmax threshold of 3.13 provided 90.9% specificity (AUC 0.79). The simplified 4-ROI method showed excellent agreement with whole-liver segmentation for background-corrected SUVmean (ICC 0.96, Lin's CCC 0.95, no significant proportional bias) and statistically equivalent diagnostic performance (DeLong p ≥ 0.33). Among discrepant cases, molecular imaging correctly reclassified the majority of patients in whom elastography and FAPI PET disagreed, which was confirmed by repeat TE or biopsy. Conclusion This prospective study provides evidence that [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT is a reliable non-invasive biomarker of hepatic stellate cell activation, that outperforms conventional methods in clinically discrepant cases of liver fibrosis, while offering whole-liver imaging that is less affected by common confounders. It reliably excludes advanced fibrosis and may help avoid unnecessary liver biopsy. These findings position FAPI PET as a problem-solving tool in CLD management.

title: UTR-Track: unscented trajectory reconstruction with re-identification for robust lesion tracking in endoscopy videos.
abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy is an important imaging modality for the screening and diagnosis of diseases in the GI tract. A lesion tracking technique helps maintain the identity and location of an abnormal region over time, enabling consistent monitoring rather than independent frame-by-frame detection. However, the complex endoscopic environment as non-linear camera displacement, soft tissue deformation, and occlusions are challenges for existing Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) methods. To address these issues, we propose UTR-Track, a robust tracking framework that integrates deep state estimation with adaptive feature learning. The method introduces OSNet-DCN, which embeds Deformable Convolutions into an Omni-Scale Network to extract deformation-robust features, coupled with a dual-tracker architecture, named VTA-TL-UKF. This VTA-TL-UKF utilizes an Unscented Kalman Filter with transfer-learning-based covariance stabilization and a Virtual Trajectory Augmentation module to recover fragmented tracks. Extensive experiments on self-collected clinical sequences and a public Hyper-Kvasir dataset with five types of the lesions such as gastric cancer (GC), esophageal cancer (EC), duodenal bulb ulcer (DBU), reflux esophagitis (RE), and gastritis, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. On the 18 annotated IGH evaluation sequence, using the primary configuration, pairing the tracker with the hybrid-trained appearance model OSNet-DCN[Formula: see text], UTR-Track reaches a Multi-Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA) of 45.4% and an IDF1 score of 74.2%. The proposed tracker eliminates identity switches IDs = 0 while improving recall (60.6%) and precision (79.9%), significantly enhancing track continuity for longitudinal lesion monitoring. These results suggest that UTR-Track effectively bridges the gap between static detection and temporally consistent tracking, supporting more reliable computer-aided diagnosis in endoscopy. Code and results are available at: https://github.com/shredder0812/UTR-Track .

title: Mask-aware knowledge distillation for low-latency pneumothorax classification in chest radiographs.
abstract: Accurate pneumothorax classification requires strong discrimination with low deployment cost. We developed a mask-aware knowledge distillation framework in which a mask-guided ResNet-50 teacher transferred dynamically annealed logits and lesion-weighted multilevel attention to a MobileNetV3-Small student, while masks and teacher-side components were removed at inference. A fixed stratified 20% SIIM-ACR hold-out set was reserved for testing; the remainder underwent five-fold cross-validation, with PTX-498 positives used only for training augmentation. The Mask-aware KD student achieved a mean validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of [Formula: see text], and the five-model student ensemble achieved a fixed-test AUC of 0.946 (95% confidence interval, 0.935-0.956) versus 0.950 for the teacher ensemble. Validation-selected 90% and 95% sensitivity targets yielded test sensitivities of 0.929 and 0.973. Uniform-attention KD achieved a lower AUC of 0.936. The student ensemble required 5.00 million parameters, 1.49 billion multiply-accumulate operations (MACs), and 51.00-ms single-threaded CPU latency at [Formula: see text]. Training-time lesion guidance enabled numerically similar discrimination with substantially lower inference cost. No independent external validation was performed, and generalizability across institutions, acquisition protocols, portable radiography settings, and patient populations remains uncertain; verified patient-level evaluation remains necessary before clinical translation.
